articles.title: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
articles.body:
One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.
The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.
Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.
Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”
Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman, the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”
The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.
Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning: “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”
He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.
“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.
This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.
“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”
Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.
The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards.
The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”.
Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”
Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks.
Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted.
“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”
- AI: Probably Nothing To Worry About airs on Channel 4 on 12 November at 10pm.
- The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear
   
On Thursday 15 October, join Dan Milmo and Professor Dame Wendy Hall and Stuart J. Russel as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only. Book tickets here or at guardian.live

articles.title: People Against Genocide Smash Military Satellites on Balfour Anniversary
articles.body:
Videos and images are free to use, with no credit needed
In the early hours of Monday 2nd November, on the 109th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, a 3-person People Against Genocide (PAG) team, once again successfully evaded security at the Tring site of military tech and cyber warfare company Ultra Intelligence & Communications (Ultra I&C), and gained access to the building. Once inside the facility at Icknield Way, Tring, Hertfordshire HP23 4JX, the PAG team began dismantling military equipment including military satellites. The three were arrested after allegedly causing extensive damage inside the weapons facility.
Ultra I&C are a key supplier to UAV Tactical Systems, the Leicester subsidiary of Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons maker, who produce 85% of the Israeli military’s killer drone fleet, and 80% of their land-based weaponry and equipment. Elbit boast that their deadly products are “battle-tested” on Palestinians, and they have been used against civilian populations across West Asia.
Ultra I&C claim to specialise in “AI mission solutions” and “secure battlefield communications systems”, but job listings for Ultra I&C’s Tring site show that it is a manufacturing facility. This was confirmed by a data breach in 2024, which showed that as well as working with Elbit, Ultra I&C work with the Israeli military directly. On a previous PAG raid of the Tring factory, action-takers also found, and dismantled, satellites bound for the Israeli military, which the Crown Prosecution Service claim were worth £1.3 million.
Today’s action was timed to coincide with the anniversary of the signing of the notorious Balfour Declaration, in which the British government committed itself to the establishment of a “Jewish homeland” in Palestine, leading to the Palestinian Nakba, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages, and the murder and expulsion of thousands of the country’s indigenous population. Today also marks one year since the Palestine Action prisoners began a collective hunger strike, which lasted 73 days.
Because of their involvement in the genocide in Gaza, PAG have targeted Ultra I & C facilities on a number of previous occasions. In addition to the previous action at Tring, they blockaded the Maidenead site in June, using lock-on devices, covering the Cambridge premises in blood-red paint and graffiti, at the end of July, and breaking into the Aberdeen site in August.
People Against Genocide issued the following statement:
“Our action today is timed to coincide with the 1917 signing of the bloody Balfour Declaration, in which the British government betrayed the Palestinian people. Consequently, the Palestinians suffered hundreds of attacks from Zionist terrorists, such as train and market bombings, and village massacres, which led on to the Nakba of 1948, and a further 78 years of ethnic cleansing and murder, culminating in the current genocide in Gaza, the pogroms in the West Bank, and a concerted attempt to exterminate the entire Palestinian population of Occupied Palestine.
“Not only did the British government sign away a country that was not theirs to give, they have continued to assist in the Zionist occupation of Palestine, and in the murder of its native population, right up to the present day. Chief among the other foreign actors actively assisting the genocide is, of course, Britain’s unruly offspring, the US, where Ultra I & C is headquartered. The firm is part of the military Industrial Complex, which makes billions from the slaughter of Palestinians, and uses Gaza as a testing ground. Sickeningly, Elbit Systems, who Ultra I & C supply, boast that their horrific weapons are ‘battle-tested’ on Palestinians.
“By shutting down the Tring death factory today, and dismantling the weapons inside, our action-takers are aiming to save lives in Palestine, and uphold international law. The Labour governments of both Burham and Starmer, have not only failed to do anything to stop the genocide, abandoning their commitments to international law, and to simple human decency, they have actively assisted the Israeli military, with spy flights and arms shipments. They have also targeted and criminalised those who oppose the genocide, leading to hundreds of arrests, and increasingly draconian misuse of the counter-terrorism laws to silence those who act, or even speak out. History will not forget their role, nor the international role of Britain over the centuries, and for the 109 years since the signing of the Balfour Declaration. Free Palestine!”
ENDS.
*The Aftershock distributes press releases and media packages of actions taken for Palestine. It operates independently from any protest group.
*To contact People Against Genocide directly, email info@peopleagainstgenocide.org
*People Against Genocide website: peopleagainstgenocide.org

articles.title: Democrats Rout GOP
articles.body:
Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats Vow to Use Majority to Check Trump
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the next House speaker, said his party would focus on affordability after a remarkable power shift in Congress. President Trump, speaking at the White House, focused on his renovation projects, not the midterms.
Latest
Democrats on Wednesday afternoon were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and had captured solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories across the country that left Republicans searching for a path forward in a drastically reordered Washington.
Triumphant as the scale of their wins came into sharper focus, Democrats vowed to take quick action to challenge President Trump and to aggressively investigate him and his administration. “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” promised Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader.
The party flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where around 60 votes separated the two candidates.
Mr. Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, celebrated the blue wave as an “American tsunami” and predicted Democrats would win at least 255 seats in the 435-seat chamber.
Vice President JD Vance placed the blame for the Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran, a remarkable break from Mr. Trump’s defense of his decision to attack. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Mr. Vance wrote on social media. “Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”
Mr. Trump used his first public appearance on Wednesday to speak about his ballroom from inside the construction site. He said he thought Mr. Vance’s assertion was “largely true,” but he said if he could go back, he would not have done it differently.
In a triumphant election night, Democrats surged in crucial House battlegrounds and beyond, picking off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama. They were on track to secure the largest majority in the chamber since 2008, when they won 257 seats.
Taken together, the results promised a freshly assertive Congress when it begins in January after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander.
The shock waves from the election quickly reverberated among Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a sweeping repudiation of their party.
Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.
“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”
Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide, flipping seats that had spent decades in Republican hands, did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature.
- G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.
- Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›
Democrats have flipped a second statewide office in Indiana. The A.P. called the state comptroller race for Jessica Bailey, who defeated the Republican incumbent, Elise Nieshalla. The comptroller had been referred to as the state auditor until a recent law change.
Indiana Democrats had been shut out of statewide office for years, but in the midterm elections have now won both the comptroller race and the secretary of state’s office. The party also flipped a Republican-held congressional seat in the Indianapolis suburbs and ousted several Republican state legislators, including the speaker of the House, who tried and failed last year to enact a new U.S. House map at President Trump’s request.
The race for Florida’s 27th Congressional District, in Miami-Dade County, remains too close to call, according to The Associated Press. Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican, leads Eliott Rodriguez, her Democratic challenger, by 0.46 percentage points, which, if it holds, could meet Florida’s threshold for an automatic machine recount, which is half a percentage point.
On Wednesday, the elections supervisor in the county said her office was still dealing with 202 mail ballots in the race with signature discrepancies, which voters have until Thursday afternoon to cure. The elections office is also reviewing provisional ballots, her office said. The local canvassing board will handle those matters in a meeting on Friday. If needed, the Florida secretary of state could order a recount by Saturday.
- By Peter Baker, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Nikolay Nikolov, Thomas Vollkommer, Rafaela Balster, James Surdam, Edward Vega and Rachel Buigas-Lopez
- By Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Edward Vega and Stephanie Swart
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Jon Miller, Edward Vega and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Stephanie Swart and Edward Vega
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer, James Surdam and Edward Vega
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh and Stephanie Swart
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
Representative Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat who has been in Congress for almost a decade and was accused of sexual misconduct this summer, has lost his House seat representing part of Los Angeles, according to The Associated Press. He was defeated by Angela Gonzales-Torres, an anti-establishment candidate from his own party endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America.
As his party reeled from a resounding defeat in the midterm elections, President Trump made an impromptu appearance on Wednesday at the White House, where he defended two of what he considers to be legacy-defining projects: his ballroom and the war in Iran.
Mr. Trump’s appearance at the ballroom’s construction site — his first comments to reporters since the American electorate delivered a sharp rebuke of his party and policies — was a ceremony to celebrate the raising of the final steel beam atop the structure. He delivered extensive remarks detailing the progress of the project before adding his signature to the beam. He never mentioned the results of the midterms.
“This is a special structure,” he said. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world.”
The beam-signing ceremony was the latest in a series of striking examples of the disconnect between Mr. Trump’s priorities and those of the American electorate. On Monday, the eve of the election, Mr. Trump gave a speech from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he spent nearly an hour detailing renovations he had ordered at sites around Washington rather than offer a closing argument to voters concerned by his handling of the economy and the war with Iran.
“You know, it was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign: ‘Why does Trump spend time on the White House?’” he said of his extensive renovations. “Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me, it’s relaxing.”
After adding his signature to the giant steel beam and watching workers lift it into place on Wednesday, Mr. Trump addressed questions from reporters about the election results. He said that Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that Republicans had lost the election because of the war in Iran was “largely true” because the conflict had driven up gas prices, but said that he would make the same decision again.
“The Iran thing, we had to do,” he said, “and we continue to do it.”
Mr. Trump said that he looked forward to working with the Democratic-controlled Congress that was just elected, unless the Democrats sought to be “destructive,” in which case he would exercise his veto powers.
Asked if he was worried at all about a possible impeachment, Mr. Trump said, “No, not even a little bit.”
The Democratic surge on Tuesday netted at least 330 state legislative seats, from New Hampshire to Arizona, giving the Democrats full control of 22 state governments and making them the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.
And while Washington remains divided, Democrats will have the power to make policy on health care, voting and taxation in state capitals that for years have been far beyond their control, such as Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.
In Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats will hold both statehouse chambers as well as the governorship. The party was on the verge of the same “trifecta” in Arizona as well.
“Our victories have shattered Republicans’ grip on our statehouses,” said Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.
The victories in state legislative races rarely grab national headlines, but statehouses exert enormous influence on issues that directly affect day-to-day life, from health care coverage to transportation. Some of those wins were the fruits of long rebuilding efforts. In Wisconsin, the fight to dismantle a Republican gerrymander of legislative districts finally delivered the Democrats both the State Senate and House, while the party retained the governor's mansion in Madison.
Elsewhere, state-level victories were almost incidental consequences of a wave that was bigger than even the most optimistic Democrat has anticipated.
The Arizona Senate’s minority leader, Priya Sundareshan, went to sleep Tuesday night with a statement saying she looks forward to seeing the votes counted. By morning, it was clear the changes would be huge.
”I’m really excited to be in the driver’s seat,” Ms. Sundareshan said.
Even in several states where Democrats did not win a majority, they still won enough seats to prevent Republican supermajorities, which confer the ability to override a governor’s veto.
Most notable were Iowa, where Rob Sand, a Democrat, won the governor’s race, and Ohio, where, Amy Acton, also a Democrat, was elected governor. They are their states’ first Democratic governors in 16 years, and with no Republican supermajority, both will have more leverage than they would otherwise have had.
State legislators allocate billions of dollars for schools, prisons and health care, and can shape policies on everything from data centers to taxes before Congress does. In Wisconsin, one of 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid access under the Affordable Care Act, Democrats now have the power to do so. But even in Texas and Georgia, the new Democratic governor and the one Democratic chamber will almost certainly apply enormous pressure to expand Medicaid as citizens struggle with health care costs.
And while legislative elections are typically overshadowed by midterm races for governor and Congress, this year’s races did command more attention, and money, in part because of the frenzied mid-decade U.S. House redistricting. Now the question of redistricting moves to the 2028 election, and the prospect of redrawing even more congressional maps, this time by Democrats.
The weakening of the Voting Rights Act by the Supreme Court in April had raised the prospects of states such as Texas and Georgia taking up redistricting again with an eye on diluting Democratic districts drawn to give Black and Hispanic voters more power. Now that those states have divided governments, a Republican redistricting would be impossible.
But Wisconsin and Pennsylvania could turn the tables on Republicans if their Democratic leaders choose to.
The earliest tally of state legislative results has Democrats netting at least 330 statehouse seats, but the number is sure to climb, perhaps as high as 800 seats. There is little doubt they will outperform 2018, when they gained more than 300 during Mr. Trump’s first term.
It was likely the best Democratic result since they gained more than 600 seats in 1974, right after Watergate, said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Republicans gingerly pointed to President Trump’s abysmal approval ratings and the same headwinds of inflation, war and fuel costs that cost them the U.S. House and Senate, but also to governor’s races that went badly for the G.O.P.
“The national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends,” Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee, said in a statement.
It remains to be seen whether the final tally will be as seismic as 2010, when Republicans unleashed their Redistricting Majority Project, or Redmap, and flipped 22 chambers and more than 700 seats — a “shellacking,” as former President Barack Obama described it.
That pendulum swing enabled Republicans to redraw maps and over the next decade to enact conservative policies to weaken labor unions, cut taxes, restrict voter access and expand education vouchers.
The president’s party has lost statehouse seats in 20 of the last 22 midterms, so Tuesday’s results were hardly a surprise, though a year ago the Republican State Leadership Committee held out hope for gains in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. Insead, all three of those statehouses will be completely in Democratic hands all with Democratic governors.
Democrats have done well in special elections to fill state legislative seats, but Democratic voters historically have chosen candidates at the top of the ticket, while leaving down- ballot races blank. That was not the case, however, on Tuesday.
And on a night full of unexpected results, one standout was North Carolina. Only three years ago, Democratic legislators were in a superminority, after State Representative Tricia Cotham, a Democrat, switched parties and have Republicans the power to override former Gov. Roy Cooper’s veto and enact the state’s most restrictive abortion policy in 50 years.
After the Democrats broke that North Carolina supermajority in 2024, their goal for this year’s midterms was simply to chip away at the Republican majority in one of the country’s most gerrymandered states.
Instead, bolstered by Mr. Cooper’s resounding victory for U.S. Senate, they seized control of the House and narrowed the gap in the Senate, bolstering Mr. Cooper’s Democratic successor, Gov. Josh Stein. Ms. Cotham lost her seat.
A similar dynamic unfolded in Georgia and Texas, where Democrats won both state’s Houses of the Representatives for the first time since the early 2000s, as part of a sweep of all statewide races, as well as the governorships
History was also on the verge of being made in Arizona, as Democrats appeared poised to claim both the House and Senate, as one of six new trifectas. Arizona Democrats have not had an outright majority in any chamber since the early 1990s, and not had full control since the mid-1960s.
And though Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont, a popular moderate Republican, won a record sixth term, statehouse Democrats regained the supermajority they had lost in 2024.
Victories by Mr. Scott and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were among the few bright spots for Republicans. They also held firm in conservative strongholds like Wyoming, Montana, Idaho and the Dakotas.
Still, there were cracks in Republican redoubts. In Missouri, Democrats broke the supermajority in both the House and Senate. And in Arkansas, Democrats gained a projected 10 seats in the State House.
Last week, Jay Morgan, a former chairman of the Georgia Republican Party, said the national outlook looked dire.
“There’s the potential of a total washout,” he said. “There are seats in play that nobody thought would be in play.”
He was proved right.
Sejal Govindarao contributed reporting.
Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the broad shift in support that Republicans saw in 2024.
The reversal was most notable among young voters and voters of color, particularly Hispanic voters, who swung toward the Democratic Party by nearly 30 percentage points. Democrats also made sizable gains among groups typically seen as stalwarts of the Republican base — white voters without a college degree and older voters — both of which swung left.
An unusual situation is brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.
The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, leads the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 65 votes as of Wednesday afternoon — an incredibly tight race that would trigger an automatic recount in dozens of other states.
In fact, 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.
Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.
There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.
Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.
Representative Richard Hudson, the North Carolina Republican who is the chairman of House Republicans’ campaign arm, conceded his election in a statement on Wednesday. Though The Associated Press has not called his race, Hudson currently trails by about 2 percentage points.
Hudson, who oversaw his party’s efforts to help House Republicans keep their majority, said in a statement that “the voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice, and I respect it.” His loss reflected the extent of Republicans’ troubles on Election Day: Trump carried his district by about 16 points in the 2024 presidential election.
President Trump spent much of the past two years promising to bring down energy prices.
Instead, his war with Iran, as well as other policies, drove up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time his administration worked to thwart efforts to fight climate change, blocking renewable energy investments that could have reduced the country’s reliance on fossil fuels or brought down costs.
On Tuesday, voters’ frustration with soaring energy prices helped propel Democrats to a blowout, with Republicans losing control of the House and the Senate, as well as the governorships of many historically conservative states.
“It’s quite clear that energy and energy affordability in particular played a big role in the electorate’s decision-making last night,” said Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a clean energy finance company.
Many Americans said concerns about the cost of gas and electricity informed their voting choices, according to polling from The Associated Press. Gasoline prices across the country were at a record high for an Election Day, according to AAA.
No single action had a bigger effect on energy costs than Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and global flows of oil disrupted, gasoline prices in the United States have jumped more than 40 percent since the war began. Diesel prices are up nearly 70 percent.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said that launching the war was among the worst decisions Mr. Trump could have made if he was trying to bring down energy costs. “It’s Econ 101 that invading Iran when they control the Strait of Hormuz is going to impact gas prices,” she said.
Daniel Raimi, a fellow at Resources for the Future, a nonprofit research institute, noted that “usually presidents have very little sway over global oil prices, but that was not the case this time.” The Iran war, he said, not only increased fuel prices but also costs for fertilizer “and a whole host of commodities.”
Beyond the war in Iran, the Trump administration has taken a sweeping approach to reshaping the nation’s energy policy, including actions that may have increased costs for consumers.
At a time when electricity demand and prices are soaring because of the data center boom, the administration has blocked the construction of offshore wind farms, despite pleas from governors to allow the projects to get built. It also mandated that coal-burning power plans stay online, even though utilities said that doing so would raise prices for their customers.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said on Wednesday that higher energy costs were a factor with voters. “Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs: on electricity, on health care, on goods,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump.
If there was one energy-related issue beyond Iran that broke through, Mr. Raimi said, it was likely higher electricity prices, which many Americans blame on the proliferation of data centers. “Voters are certainly unhappy about higher electricity bills, but the larger driver for those higher prices is increased demand,” he said.
While data centers have become deeply unpopular with voters, Mr. Trump and his administration have offered stalwart support for the industry and dismissed voters’ concerns about them.
Other issues, like keeping coal plants open or blocking wind farms, he said, were less important in the voting booth because their effect on prices would be marginal.
Some of the Democrats who won seized on energy affordability as part of their campaigns. Roy Cooper, who flipped a Republican Senate seat in North Carolina, said at a campaign stop that the war in Iran was “driving the cost of gas through the roof.”
James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas in decades, has called for suspending the federal gas tax and diesel tax.
And Abdul El-Sayed, who won a Senate seat in Michigan, touted the need to adopt clean energy. “We have all the technology we need to drop the price of electricity via renewable energy,” he said at a recent event. “And all of those renewable energy investments, guess what? They create really great jobs.”
While Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, bringing down energy prices is unlikely to be swift or easy.
Mr. Trump has two years left in office. In recent weeks, he has indicated that he might intensify attacks in Iran following the midterm election, which could lead to further spikes in oil prices.
But with voters signaling their frustration with the high cost of gas, diesel and electricity, some clean-energy supporters said they believed even Mr. Trump might be open to revising his stance on some issues that have driven up prices.
“The election was a compete repudiation of his energy agenda,” said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an environmental group. “The question is what comes next, and one thing he could do is stop blocking clean power that could help meet demand and lower costs.”
Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the Senate in the next Congress, the party’s largest majority since at least 2012, and at least 237 seats in the House, with the potential for that number to grow significantly once more races are called. If Democrats end up with more than 257 seats, it would be the largest majority for either party in that chamber since 1992.
Black voters remained the backbone of the Democratic coalition across the South in this year’s election. House Democratic candidates won Black voters by a margin of roughly 80 percentage points nationwide, according to Times Voter Trends. That was an increase from 2024, when the Democrats’ presidential candidate, Kamala Harris, won Black voters by about 70 points.
The Democrats expanded their overwhelming margins among Black voters in several Southern states, among them Mississippi, South Carolina, Georgia, North Carolina, Louisiana and Alabama.
But some of the more striking movement came among white voters, who shifted toward Democrats by 12 points in Mississippi, 15 points in Alabama and 19 points in North Carolina.
Starting last summer, President Trump pushed Republicans to engage in an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting project to overhaul congressional maps in favor of the G.O.P. The goal was to protect a House majority during his final two years in office.
It did not work.
Instead, Democrats on Tuesday gained at least eight seats in Republican-run states that had redistricted over the past 16 months. It was a stiff rebuff for a plan to sort just enough Republicans into just enough districts to give the party a 20-seat House firewall.
Months of political warfare, including more than $200 million in spending on referendums in California and Virginia, simply did not anticipate an electorate that backed House Democratic candidates by 13 percentage points.
No map could have produced a Republican advantage strong enough to withstand such a Democratic wave.
“Donald Trump and Republicans poked the bear, and they got mauled,” said John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. “There’s no way to look at this cycle and not see that the scheme to gerrymander the country was a complete and utter catastrophe.”
The plan’s demise illustrated once again the perpetual elasticity of the American electorate. Just as the coalitions that elected Barack Obama president in 2008 had evaporated by 2010, groups that backed Mr. Trump in 2024 abandoned him for 2026.
On Wednesday, House Democratic leaders crowed about defeating the Republican redistricting. They stood in front of a poster featuring a May social media post from James Blair, who ran Mr. Trump’s political operation, in which he boasted that redistricting would net the G.O.P. 16 seats.
“The American people hate it when politicians try to pick their voters,” said Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, who leads the House Democrats’ campaign arm.
It will take weeks and precinct-level analysis of election results to determine whether Republicans would have won more seats had they not redistricted at all. But Adam Kincaid, the executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust, said on Wednesday that without redrawn maps, his party likely would have lost five more House seats than it did.
He also said Democrats likely cost themselves two House seats in California that they could have won with the 2024 map.
Perhaps nowhere better demonstrated the futility of the Republicans’ plans than Texas and North Carolina. Texas Republicans anticipated that the Hispanic swing toward Mr. Trump in 2024 would be durable. Instead, five districts in Hispanic-heavy South Texas moved to Democrats.
North Carolina legislators redrew congressional lines ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections, producing a map intended to deliver 11 of the state’s 14 districts to Republicans. Though not all of Tuesday’s races have been called, Democrats appear on pace to win 10 out of the 14 seats.
In Florida, Republicans gained zero seats in a map they believed would give them four held by Democrats. An Ohio map designed to shift two seats to Republicans may have handed two more to Democrats. And new maps drawn to squeeze out Democrats in Alabama and Tennessee also failed.
At the same time, Democrats are poised to gain several seats from new California congressional districts they drew in response to the Republican effort. There also will be a new Democratic congressman in Utah, where judges ordered new maps. And White House attempts to force new districts were foiled by legislators in Indiana and Nebraska and the courts in Missouri.
It could have been worse for Republicans. The Virginia Supreme Court invalidated a voter-approved plan that likely would have handed 10 of the state’s 11 congressional seats to Democrats. Under the existing map, Democrats are likely to win eight.
The redistricting fight is likely not over. Democrats on Tuesday won control of state governments in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, which could redraw maps to secure seats for their party.
Maryland voters approved a referendum to allow legislators to draw the state’s one Republican House district out of existence. And Republicans may still attempt new maps in South Carolina and Mississippi.
Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, who lost his bid for a fourth term, could call a special session before the year’s end and ask legislators for yet another new map that could help Republicans recoup their losses.
In Georgia, however, Gov. Brian Kemp said Wednesday morning that he would not call a special session to redistrict before he hands over control to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Annie Karni contributed reporting.
William Lawrence, a Democrat and climate activist, scored a marquee victory for the ascendant progressive movement, ousting Representative Tom Barrett, a first-term Republican, to flip a battleground seat in central Michigan, according to The Associated Press. Lawrence campaigned on expanding access to government-funded health care and opposing data centers, issues that progressives have argued could energize working-class voters, not just in Democratic primaries but also in general elections.
Laura Gillen, a one-term Democratic incumbent, fended off a challenge from the Republican Jeanine Driscoll, the receiver of taxes for the town of Hempstead, according to The Associated Press. Gillen will continue to represent New York’s Fourth Congressional District, which includes portions of Nassau County on Long Island.
Formerly the town supervisor in Hempstead, Gillen narrowly defeated a Republican incumbent, Anthony D’Esposito, to flip the seat in 2024.
Tom Suozzi, a Democratic incumbent, won re-election in New York’s Third Congressional District, defeating the Republican Mike LiPetri, according to The Associated Press. In 2024, Suozzi narrowly won a tough battle for the Long Island district, which includes a small portion of Queens.
Suozzi was first elected to the district in 2016, vacated his seat to run for governor in 2022 and reclaimed it two years ago. Both candidates emphasized bipartisanship on the campaign trail this year.
Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the two-term Democrat from a conservative-leaning rural district in Washington State, won her re-election bid, according to The Associated Press. She holds on to one of the most competitive seats in the country, defeating a Republican who had tried to distance himself from President Trump in a bid to appeal to independent voters.
Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 House Republican, announced that he would run to be the minority leader in the next Congress. Scalise, who has been in House Republican leadership since 2014, emphasized his experience in a letter to his colleagues. He called for “substantive changes to the way our conference operates,” arguing that the G.O.P. needed to be more unified in its approach.
Scalise’s announcement will pit him once again against Representative Jim Jordan, the firebrand, hard-line conservative from Ohio. Both men ran for speaker in 2023, but neither of them was able to secure the necessary support to win.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the governor-elect of Tennessee, declined to say on Wednesday whom she will name to fill her vacant seat in the Senate, calling it a conversation for another day. Rumors have circulated in recent days about who might get the nod. One possibility is Pete Hegseth, the current Pentagon chief who is a Tennessee resident.
Trump ended his public appearance at the White House after about half an hour, during which he focused on renovation projects and appeared to have little interest in discussing the midterms. He did not mention the Republican defeat last night in his remarks until asked by reporters afterward, then defended his campaign strategy. He supported Vice President JD Vance’s social media post that said the Iran War was responsible for Republicans’ electoral loss, but the president also repeatedly suggested he had no regrets on the war, and would do it all again.
“As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” he said.
Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia shut down speculation on Wednesday that he would call a special legislative session to rush through new congressional maps favorable to Republicans or weaken the powers of his office before his Democratic successor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, could assume it.
“The voters of our state have spoken,” Mr. Kemp, a two-term Republican incumbent leaving office because of term limits, said in a statement on Wednesday morning. “As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state.”
A Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act has prompted Republican lawmakers across the South to redraw federal and state legislative boundaries to benefit their party, eliminating districts that had been created to promote minority representation.
Georgia’s legislature had resisted doing that, despite calls from President Trump and some Republicans in the state to take action. Mr. Kemp declined to redraw maps before the midterm elections, noting that early voting in the primaries had, by that point, already started.
He then called a special session in June to draw up new maps for the 2028 election. But less than an hour after the session began, Republican legislative leaders came out and said they would not present new maps after all.
They cited a desire for a methodical process that would include greater input from voters, rather than rushing legislation through, but the decision was also a recognition of mounting protests against redistricting and fears that moving forward could undermine their party’s already enfeebled fortunes in the midterm elections.
There was also an implicit expectation among many political observers that the matter had been shelved only temporarily, and that a narrow window between the election and when a new governor takes power would provide an opportunity not only to enact new maps but also to strip away some of the authority of the governor’s office. The chatter intensified as polls indicated a greater possibility of victory for Ms. Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta and the first Democrat to be elected governor of Georgia in more than 25 years.
Mr. Kemp moved immediately to cut off that possibility, but he said there were “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before the convening of the regular session in January.”
After several minutes of watching a beam being lifted to the ceiling, Trump went back to taking questions. He was asked if he knew Vice President JD Vance was going to make the lengthy, critical post he made this morning. “I know how he feels about it, I think it was fine,” he said, calling the post “good.” He said he had spoken to Vance but did not elaborate much.
Trump said he couldn’t predict who would run for president in 2028. “Maybe he won’t run, I don’t know who’s going to run,” he said.
Trump spoke ambiguously of his future relationship with the Democrat-controlled Congress that was just elected. “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” he said, noting he had “the power to veto.” Trump said much the same thing last night, saying in an interview with The Times that he was looking forward to working with Democrats, but also posting an image with the word “VETO” shortly after.

articles.title: Democrats Rout GOP
articles.body:
Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats Vow to Use Majority to Check Trump
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the next House speaker, said his party would focus on affordability after a remarkable power shift in Congress. President Trump, speaking at the White House, focused on his renovation projects, not the midterms.
Latest
Democrats on Wednesday afternoon were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and had captured solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories across the country that left Republicans searching for a path forward in a drastically reordered Washington.
Triumphant as the scale of their wins came into sharper focus, Democrats vowed to take quick action to challenge President Trump and to aggressively investigate him and his administration. “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” promised Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader.
The party flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where around 60 votes separated the two candidates.
Mr. Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, celebrated the blue wave as an “American tsunami” and predicted Democrats would win at least 255 seats in the 435-seat chamber.
Vice President JD Vance placed the blame for the Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran, a remarkable break from Mr. Trump’s defense of his decision to attack. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Mr. Vance wrote on social media. “Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”
Mr. Trump used his first public appearance on Wednesday to speak about his ballroom from inside the construction site. He said he thought Mr. Vance’s assertion was “largely true,” but he said if he could go back, he would not have done it differently.
In a triumphant election night, Democrats surged in crucial House battlegrounds and beyond, picking off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama. They were on track to secure the largest majority in the chamber since 2008, when they won 257 seats.
Taken together, the results promised a freshly assertive Congress when it begins in January after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander.
The shock waves from the election quickly reverberated among Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a sweeping repudiation of their party.
Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.
“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”
Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide, flipping seats that had spent decades in Republican hands, did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature.
- G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.
- Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›
Democrats have flipped a second statewide office in Indiana. The A.P. called the state comptroller race for Jessica Bailey, who defeated the Republican incumbent, Elise Nieshalla. The comptroller had been referred to as the state auditor until a recent law change.
Indiana Democrats had been shut out of statewide office for years, but in the midterm elections have now won both the comptroller race and the secretary of state’s office. The party also flipped a Republican-held congressional seat in the Indianapolis suburbs and ousted several Republican state legislators, including the speaker of the House, who tried and failed last year to enact a new U.S. House map at President Trump’s request.
The race for Florida’s 27th Congressional District, in Miami-Dade County, remains too close to call, according to The Associated Press. Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican, leads Eliott Rodriguez, her Democratic challenger, by 0.46 percentage points, which, if it holds, could meet Florida’s threshold for an automatic machine recount, which is half a percentage point.
On Wednesday, the elections supervisor in the county said her office was still dealing with 202 mail ballots in the race with signature discrepancies, which voters have until Thursday afternoon to cure. The elections office is also reviewing provisional ballots, her office said. The local canvassing board will handle those matters in a meeting on Friday. If needed, the Florida secretary of state could order a recount by Saturday.
- By Peter Baker, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Nikolay Nikolov, Thomas Vollkommer, Rafaela Balster, James Surdam, Edward Vega and Rachel Buigas-Lopez
- By Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Edward Vega and Stephanie Swart
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Jon Miller, Edward Vega and James Surdam
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Stephanie Swart and Edward Vega
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
- By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer, James Surdam and Edward Vega
- By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh and Stephanie Swart
- By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega
Representative Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat who has been in Congress for almost a decade and was accused of sexual misconduct this summer, has lost his House seat representing part of Los Angeles, according to The Associated Press. He was defeated by Angela Gonzales-Torres, an anti-establishment candidate from his own party endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America.
As his party reeled from a resounding defeat in the midterm elections, President Trump made an impromptu appearance on Wednesday at the White House, where he defended two of what he considers to be legacy-defining projects: his ballroom and the war in Iran.
Mr. Trump’s appearance at the ballroom’s construction site — his first comments to reporters since the American electorate delivered a sharp rebuke of his party and policies — was a ceremony to celebrate the raising of the final steel beam atop the structure. He delivered extensive remarks detailing the progress of the project before adding his signature to the beam. He never mentioned the results of the midterms.
“This is a special structure,” he said. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world.”
The beam-signing ceremony was the latest in a series of striking examples of the disconnect between Mr. Trump’s priorities and those of the American electorate. On Monday, the eve of the election, Mr. Trump gave a speech from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he spent nearly an hour detailing renovations he had ordered at sites around Washington rather than offer a closing argument to voters concerned by his handling of the economy and the war with Iran.
“You know, it was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign: ‘Why does Trump spend time on the White House?’” he said of his extensive renovations. “Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me, it’s relaxing.”
After adding his signature to the giant steel beam and watching workers lift it into place on Wednesday, Mr. Trump addressed questions from reporters about the election results. He said that Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that Republicans had lost the election because of the war in Iran was “largely true” because the conflict had driven up gas prices, but said that he would make the same decision again.
“The Iran thing, we had to do,” he said, “and we continue to do it.”
Mr. Trump said that he looked forward to working with the Democratic-controlled Congress that was just elected, unless the Democrats sought to be “destructive,” in which case he would exercise his veto powers.
Asked if he was worried at all about a possible impeachment, Mr. Trump said, “No, not even a little bit.”
The Democratic surge on Tuesday netted at least 330 state legislative seats, from New Hampshire to Arizona, giving the Democrats full control of 22 state governments and making them the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.
And while Washington remains divided, Democrats will have the power to make policy on health care, voting and taxation in state capitals that for years have been far beyond their control, such as Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.
In Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats will hold both statehouse chambers as well as the governorship. The party was on the verge of the same “trifecta” in Arizona as well.
“Our victories have shattered Republicans’ grip on our statehouses,” said Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.
The victories in state legislative races rarely grab national headlines, but statehouses exert enormous influence on issues that directly affect day-to-day life, from health care coverage to transportation. Some of those wins were the fruits of long rebuilding efforts. In Wisconsin, the fight to dismantle a Republican gerrymander of legislative districts finally delivered the Democrats both the State Senate and House, while the party retained the governor's mansion in Madison.
Elsewhere, state-level victories were almost incidental consequences of a wave that was bigger than even the most optimistic Democrat has anticipated.
The Arizona Senate’s minority leader, Priya Sundareshan, went to sleep Tuesday night with a statement saying she looks forward to seeing the votes counted. By morning, it was clear the changes would be huge.
”I’m really excited to be in the driver’s seat,” Ms. Sundareshan said.
Even in several states where Democrats did not win a majority, they still won enough seats to prevent Republican supermajorities, which confer the ability to override a governor’s veto.
Most notable were Iowa, where Rob Sand, a Democrat, won the governor’s race, and Ohio, where, Amy Acton, also a Democrat, was elected governor. They are their states’ first Democratic governors in 16 years, and with no Republican supermajority, both will have more leverage than they would otherwise have had.
State legislators allocate billions of dollars for schools, prisons and health care, and can shape policies on everything from data centers to taxes before Congress does. In Wisconsin, one of 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid access under the Affordable Care Act, Democrats now have the power to do so. But even in Texas and Georgia, the new Democratic governor and the one Democratic chamber will almost certainly apply enormous pressure to expand Medicaid as citizens struggle with health care costs.
And while legislative elections are typically overshadowed by midterm races for governor and Congress, this year’s races did command more attention, and money, in part because of the frenzied mid-decade U.S. House redistricting. Now the question of redistricting moves to the 2028 election, and the prospect of redrawing even more congressional maps, this time by Democrats.
The weakening of the Voting Rights Act by the Supreme Court in April had raised the prospects of states such as Texas and Georgia taking up redistricting again with an eye on diluting Democratic districts drawn to give Black and Hispanic voters more power. Now that those states have divided governments, a Republican redistricting would be impossible.
But Wisconsin and Pennsylvania could turn the tables on Republicans if their Democratic leaders choose to.
The earliest tally of state legislative results has Democrats netting at least 330 statehouse seats, but the number is sure to climb, perhaps as high as 800 seats. There is little doubt they will outperform 2018, when they gained more than 300 during Mr. Trump’s first term.
It was likely the best Democratic result since they gained more than 600 seats in 1974, right after Watergate, said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Republicans gingerly pointed to President Trump’s abysmal approval ratings and the same headwinds of inflation, war and fuel costs that cost them the U.S. House and Senate, but also to governor’s races that went badly for the G.O.P.
“The national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends,” Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee, said in a statement.
It remains to be seen whether the final tally will be as seismic as 2010, when Republicans unleashed their Redistricting Majority Project, or Redmap, and flipped 22 chambers and more than 700 seats — a “shellacking,” as former President Barack Obama described it.
That pendulum swing enabled Republicans to redraw maps and over the next decade to enact conservative policies to weaken labor unions, cut taxes, restrict voter access and expand education vouchers.
The president’s party has lost statehouse seats in 20 of the last 22 midterms, so Tuesday’s results were hardly a surprise, though a year ago the Republican State Leadership Committee held out hope for gains in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. Insead, all three of those statehouses will be completely in Democratic hands all with Democratic governors.
Democrats have done well in special elections to fill state legislative seats, but Democratic voters historically have chosen candidates at the top of the ticket, while leaving down- ballot races blank. That was not the case, however, on Tuesday.
And on a night full of unexpected results, one standout was North Carolina. Only three years ago, Democratic legislators were in a superminority, after State Representative Tricia Cotham, a Democrat, switched parties and have Republicans the power to override former Gov. Roy Cooper’s veto and enact the state’s most restrictive abortion policy in 50 years.
After the Democrats broke that North Carolina supermajority in 2024, their goal for this year’s midterms was simply to chip away at the Republican majority in one of the country’s most gerrymandered states.
Instead, bolstered by Mr. Cooper’s resounding victory for U.S. Senate, they seized control of the House and narrowed the gap in the Senate, bolstering Mr. Cooper’s Democratic successor, Gov. Josh Stein. Ms. Cotham lost her seat.
A similar dynamic unfolded in Georgia and Texas, where Democrats won both state’s Houses of the Representatives for the first time since the early 2000s, as part of a sweep of all statewide races, as well as the governorships
History was also on the verge of being made in Arizona, as Democrats appeared poised to claim both the House and Senate, as one of six new trifectas. Arizona Democrats have not had an outright majority in any chamber since the early 1990s, and not had full control since the mid-1960s.
And though Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont, a popular moderate Republican, won a record sixth term, statehouse Democrats regained the supermajority they had lost in 2024.
Victories by Mr. Scott and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were among the few bright spots for Republicans. They also held firm in conservative strongholds like Wyoming, Montana, Idaho and the Dakotas.
Still, there were cracks in Republican redoubts. In Missouri, Democrats broke the supermajority in both the House and Senate. And in Arkansas, Democrats gained a projected 10 seats in the State House.
Last week, Jay Morgan, a former chairman of the Georgia Republican Party, said the national outlook looked dire.
“There’s the potential of a total washout,” he said. “There are seats in play that nobody thought would be in play.”
He was proved right.
Sejal Govindarao contributed reporting.
Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the broad shift in support that Republicans saw in 2024.
The reversal was most notable among young voters and voters of color, particularly Hispanic voters, who swung toward the Democratic Party by nearly 30 percentage points. Democrats also made sizable gains among groups typically seen as stalwarts of the Republican base — white voters without a college degree and older voters — both of which swung left.
An unusual situation is brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.
The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, leads the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 65 votes as of Wednesday afternoon — an incredibly tight race that would trigger an automatic recount in dozens of other states.
In fact, 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.
Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.
There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.
Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.
Representative Richard Hudson, the North Carolina Republican who is the chairman of House Republicans’ campaign arm, conceded his election in a statement on Wednesday. Though The Associated Press has not called his race, Hudson currently trails by about 2 percentage points.
Hudson, who oversaw his party’s efforts to help House Republicans keep their majority, said in a statement that “the voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice, and I respect it.” His loss reflected the extent of Republicans’ troubles on Election Day: Trump carried his district by about 16 points in the 2024 presidential election.
President Trump spent much of the past two years promising to bring down energy prices.
Instead, his war with Iran, as well as other policies, drove up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time his administration worked to thwart efforts to fight climate change, blocking renewable energy investments that could have reduced the country’s reliance on fossil fuels or brought down costs.
On Tuesday, voters’ frustration with soaring energy prices helped propel Democrats to a blowout, with Republicans losing control of the House and the Senate, as well as the governorships of many historically conservative states.
“It’s quite clear that energy and energy affordability in particular played a big role in the electorate’s decision-making last night,” said Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a clean energy finance company.
Many Americans said concerns about the cost of gas and electricity informed their voting choices, according to polling from The Associated Press. Gasoline prices across the country were at a record high for an Election Day, according to AAA.
No single action had a bigger effect on energy costs than Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and global flows of oil disrupted, gasoline prices in the United States have jumped more than 40 percent since the war began. Diesel prices are up nearly 70 percent.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said that launching the war was among the worst decisions Mr. Trump could have made if he was trying to bring down energy costs. “It’s Econ 101 that invading Iran when they control the Strait of Hormuz is going to impact gas prices,” she said.
Daniel Raimi, a fellow at Resources for the Future, a nonprofit research institute, noted that “usually presidents have very little sway over global oil prices, but that was not the case this time.” The Iran war, he said, not only increased fuel prices but also costs for fertilizer “and a whole host of commodities.”
Beyond the war in Iran, the Trump administration has taken a sweeping approach to reshaping the nation’s energy policy, including actions that may have increased costs for consumers.
At a time when electricity demand and prices are soaring because of the data center boom, the administration has blocked the construction of offshore wind farms, despite pleas from governors to allow the projects to get built. It also mandated that coal-burning power plans stay online, even though utilities said that doing so would raise prices for their customers.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said on Wednesday that higher energy costs were a factor with voters. “Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs: on electricity, on health care, on goods,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump.
If there was one energy-related issue beyond Iran that broke through, Mr. Raimi said, it was likely higher electricity prices, which many Americans blame on the proliferation of data centers. “Voters are certainly unhappy about higher electricity bills, but the larger driver for those higher prices is increased demand,” he said.
While data centers have become deeply unpopular with voters, Mr. Trump and his administration have offered stalwart support for the industry and dismissed voters’ concerns about them.
Other issues, like keeping coal plants open or blocking wind farms, he said, were less important in the voting booth because their effect on prices would be marginal.
Some of the Democrats who won seized on energy affordability as part of their campaigns. Roy Cooper, who flipped a Republican Senate seat in North Carolina, said at a campaign stop that the war in Iran was “driving the cost of gas through the roof.”
James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas in decades, has called for suspending the federal gas tax and diesel tax.
And Abdul El-Sayed, who won a Senate seat in Michigan, touted the need to adopt clean energy. “We have all the technology we need to drop the price of electricity via renewable energy,” he said at a recent event. “And all of those renewable energy investments, guess what? They create really great jobs.”
While Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, bringing down energy prices is unlikely to be swift or easy.
Mr. Trump has two years left in office. In recent weeks, he has indicated that he might intensify attacks in Iran following the midterm election, which could lead to further spikes in oil prices.
But with voters signaling their frustration with the high cost of gas, diesel and electricity, some clean-energy supporters said they believed even Mr. Trump might be open to revising his stance on some issues that have driven up prices.
“The election was a compete repudiation of his energy agenda,” said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an environmental group. “The question is what comes next, and one thing he could do is stop blocking clean power that could help meet demand and lower costs.”
Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the Senate in the next Congress, the party’s largest majority since at least 2012, and at least 237 seats in the House, with the potential for that number to grow significantly once more races are called. If Democrats end up with more than 257 seats, it would be the largest majority for either party in that chamber since 1992.
Black voters remained the backbone of the Democratic coalition across the South in this year’s election. House Democratic candidates won Black voters by a margin of roughly 80 percentage points nationwide, according to Times Voter Trends. That was an increase from 2024, when the Democrats’ presidential candidate, Kamala Harris, won Black voters by about 70 points.
The Democrats expanded their overwhelming margins among Black voters in several Southern states, among them Mississippi, South Carolina, Georgia, North Carolina, Louisiana and Alabama.
But some of the more striking movement came among white voters, who shifted toward Democrats by 12 points in Mississippi, 15 points in Alabama and 19 points in North Carolina.
Starting last summer, President Trump pushed Republicans to engage in an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting project to overhaul congressional maps in favor of the G.O.P. The goal was to protect a House majority during his final two years in office.
It did not work.
Instead, Democrats on Tuesday gained at least eight seats in Republican-run states that had redistricted over the past 16 months. It was a stiff rebuff for a plan to sort just enough Republicans into just enough districts to give the party a 20-seat House firewall.
Months of political warfare, including more than $200 million in spending on referendums in California and Virginia, simply did not anticipate an electorate that backed House Democratic candidates by 13 percentage points.
No map could have produced a Republican advantage strong enough to withstand such a Democratic wave.
“Donald Trump and Republicans poked the bear, and they got mauled,” said John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. “There’s no way to look at this cycle and not see that the scheme to gerrymander the country was a complete and utter catastrophe.”
The plan’s demise illustrated once again the perpetual elasticity of the American electorate. Just as the coalitions that elected Barack Obama president in 2008 had evaporated by 2010, groups that backed Mr. Trump in 2024 abandoned him for 2026.
On Wednesday, House Democratic leaders crowed about defeating the Republican redistricting. They stood in front of a poster featuring a May social media post from James Blair, who ran Mr. Trump’s political operation, in which he boasted that redistricting would net the G.O.P. 16 seats.
“The American people hate it when politicians try to pick their voters,” said Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, who leads the House Democrats’ campaign arm.
It will take weeks and precinct-level analysis of election results to determine whether Republicans would have won more seats had they not redistricted at all. But Adam Kincaid, the executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust, said on Wednesday that without redrawn maps, his party likely would have lost five more House seats than it did.
He also said Democrats likely cost themselves two House seats in California that they could have won with the 2024 map.
Perhaps nowhere better demonstrated the futility of the Republicans’ plans than Texas and North Carolina. Texas Republicans anticipated that the Hispanic swing toward Mr. Trump in 2024 would be durable. Instead, five districts in Hispanic-heavy South Texas moved to Democrats.
North Carolina legislators redrew congressional lines ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections, producing a map intended to deliver 11 of the state’s 14 districts to Republicans. Though not all of Tuesday’s races have been called, Democrats appear on pace to win 10 out of the 14 seats.
In Florida, Republicans gained zero seats in a map they believed would give them four held by Democrats. An Ohio map designed to shift two seats to Republicans may have handed two more to Democrats. And new maps drawn to squeeze out Democrats in Alabama and Tennessee also failed.
At the same time, Democrats are poised to gain several seats from new California congressional districts they drew in response to the Republican effort. There also will be a new Democratic congressman in Utah, where judges ordered new maps. And White House attempts to force new districts were foiled by legislators in Indiana and Nebraska and the courts in Missouri.
It could have been worse for Republicans. The Virginia Supreme Court invalidated a voter-approved plan that likely would have handed 10 of the state’s 11 congressional seats to Democrats. Under the existing map, Democrats are likely to win eight.
The redistricting fight is likely not over. Democrats on Tuesday won control of state governments in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, which could redraw maps to secure seats for their party.
Maryland voters approved a referendum to allow legislators to draw the state’s one Republican House district out of existence. And Republicans may still attempt new maps in South Carolina and Mississippi.
Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, who lost his bid for a fourth term, could call a special session before the year’s end and ask legislators for yet another new map that could help Republicans recoup their losses.
In Georgia, however, Gov. Brian Kemp said Wednesday morning that he would not call a special session to redistrict before he hands over control to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Annie Karni contributed reporting.
William Lawrence, a Democrat and climate activist, scored a marquee victory for the ascendant progressive movement, ousting Representative Tom Barrett, a first-term Republican, to flip a battleground seat in central Michigan, according to The Associated Press.
