Lawrence campaigned on expanding access to government-funded health care and opposing data centers, issues that progressives have argued could energize working-class voters, not just in Democratic primaries but also in general elections.
Laura Gillen, a one-term Democratic incumbent, fended off a challenge from the Republican Jeanine Driscoll, the receiver of taxes for the town of Hempstead, according to The Associated Press. Gillen will continue to represent New York’s Fourth Congressional District, which includes portions of Nassau County on Long Island.
Formerly the town supervisor in Hempstead, Gillen narrowly defeated a Republican incumbent, Anthony D’Esposito, to flip the seat in 2024.
Tom Suozzi, a Democratic incumbent, won re-election in New York’s Third Congressional District, defeating the Republican Mike LiPetri, according to The Associated Press. In 2024, Suozzi narrowly won a tough battle for the Long Island district, which includes a small portion of Queens.
Suozzi was first elected to the district in 2016, vacated his seat to run for governor in 2022 and reclaimed it two years ago. Both candidates emphasized bipartisanship on the campaign trail this year.
Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the two-term Democrat from a conservative-leaning rural district in Washington State, won her re-election bid, according to The Associated Press. She holds on to one of the most competitive seats in the country, defeating a Republican who had tried to distance himself from President Trump in a bid to appeal to independent voters.
Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 House Republican, announced that he would run to be the minority leader in the next Congress. Scalise, who has been in House Republican leadership since 2014, emphasized his experience in a letter to his colleagues. He called for “substantive changes to the way our conference operates,” arguing that the G.O.P. needed to be more unified in its approach.
Scalise’s announcement will pit him once again against Representative Jim Jordan, the firebrand, hard-line conservative from Ohio. Both men ran for speaker in 2023, but neither of them was able to secure the necessary support to win.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the governor-elect of Tennessee, declined to say on Wednesday whom she will name to fill her vacant seat in the Senate, calling it a conversation for another day. Rumors have circulated in recent days about who might get the nod. One possibility is Pete Hegseth, the current Pentagon chief who is a Tennessee resident.
Trump ended his public appearance at the White House after about half an hour, during which he focused on renovation projects and appeared to have little interest in discussing the midterms. He did not mention the Republican defeat last night in his remarks until asked by reporters afterward, then defended his campaign strategy. He supported Vice President JD Vance’s social media post that said the Iran War was responsible for Republicans’ electoral loss, but the president also repeatedly suggested he had no regrets on the war, and would do it all again.
“As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” he said.
Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia shut down speculation on Wednesday that he would call a special legislative session to rush through new congressional maps favorable to Republicans or weaken the powers of his office before his Democratic successor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, could assume it.
“The voters of our state have spoken,” Mr. Kemp, a two-term Republican incumbent leaving office because of term limits, said in a statement on Wednesday morning. “As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state.”
A Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act has prompted Republican lawmakers across the South to redraw federal and state legislative boundaries to benefit their party, eliminating districts that had been created to promote minority representation.
Georgia’s legislature had resisted doing that, despite calls from President Trump and some Republicans in the state to take action. Mr. Kemp declined to redraw maps before the midterm elections, noting that early voting in the primaries had, by that point, already started.
He then called a special session in June to draw up new maps for the 2028 election. But less than an hour after the session began, Republican legislative leaders came out and said they would not present new maps after all.
They cited a desire for a methodical process that would include greater input from voters, rather than rushing legislation through, but the decision was also a recognition of mounting protests against redistricting and fears that moving forward could undermine their party’s already enfeebled fortunes in the midterm elections.
There was also an implicit expectation among many political observers that the matter had been shelved only temporarily, and that a narrow window between the election and when a new governor takes power would provide an opportunity not only to enact new maps but also to strip away some of the authority of the governor’s office. The chatter intensified as polls indicated a greater possibility of victory for Ms. Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta and the first Democrat to be elected governor of Georgia in more than 25 years.
Mr. Kemp moved immediately to cut off that possibility, but he said there were “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before the convening of the regular session in January.”
After several minutes of watching a beam being lifted to the ceiling, Trump went back to taking questions. He was asked if he knew Vice President JD Vance was going to make the lengthy, critical post he made this morning. “I know how he feels about it, I think it was fine,” he said, calling the post “good.” He said he had spoken to Vance but did not elaborate much.
Trump said he couldn’t predict who would run for president in 2028. “Maybe he won’t run, I don’t know who’s going to run,” he said.
Trump spoke ambiguously of his future relationship with the Democrat-controlled Congress that was just elected. “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” he said, noting he had “the power to veto.” Trump said much the same thing last night, saying in an interview with The Times that he was looking forward to working with Democrats, but also posting an image with the word “VETO” shortly after.

articles.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
articles.body:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)
Executive summary
When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.
Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:
- Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. 
  - For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.
  - Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6. Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.
- Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.
Today we are releasing five artifacts:
- The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;
- A technical report explaining the details of our system;
- A (Claude-written) protocol specification document;
- Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and
- Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.
We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.
Introduction
When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.
However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.
The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.
One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.
Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).
The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.
We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.
Trust challenges in AI proliferation
The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).
Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.
Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.
Challenge 1: pacing
Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?
How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.
Challenge 2: tamper detection
As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3
How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.
Challenge 3: text provenance
One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?
How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.
For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).
Challenge 4: model approval
Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?
How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.
A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.
Our system: FlashProve
FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.
FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:
- In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase.
- In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:
The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.
Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.
Guarantees
A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:
- A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier.
- A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.
Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.
- A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden.
- A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure.
Evaluation
We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.
- Prover. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.
- Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.
Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.
Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.
Engineering the system
FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:
- The prover's work is proportional to the experts that actually ran. In a MoE model a token uses ~17B of the 400B parameters, and the prover's work per token is proportional to those ~17B instead of all parameters (the proof still hides which experts were chosen).
- Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request.
- The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices.
Post-hoc versus in-line
When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.
Trustworthiness from formal verification
Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?
The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:
- Completeness: if the statement is correct, the resulting proof is accepted by the verifier.
- Soundness: any fake proof is rejected by the verifier (except with negligible probability).
- Zero knowledge: the proof reveals no information about the weights of the model, beyond what the verifier can infer from the response itself.4
These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.
Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.
Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.
- For soundness, we only need the verifier code to be correct (the entire value of having “proofs” is that you can fully distrust the prover if you trust the verifier). We provide an executable Lean verifier, alongside the C++ verifier. The Lean verifier runs more slowly, but Lean proves that it accepts only what the verifier in our soundness theorem accepts. Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests.
- For completeness, the threat model does not assume adversarial attacks (the prover and verifier are honest). Therefore, a Lean verifier lets us gain confidence through standard software testing that the honest prover produces accepting proofs: run the prover on a correct statement, and then the Lean verifier on the resulting proof.
- For zero knowledge, we only need the prover to be correct. However, unlike the verifier, the prover is an expensive procedure, and it would be impractical to run a Lean prover. We do not provide facilitations here: we expect that any prover that wants to hide the weights of a model they are serving has access to enough resources for careful agentic and/or human security audits to ensure equivalence to the Lean prover.
Prior work
Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.
Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. The above numbers speak to the precipitous progress of provable inference in the past years. They should update our priors on what it is possible to prove in zero-knowledge.
- In 2024, zkLLM proved a 13B model at about 2.5 tokens/second on one A100. The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify.
- FlashProve proves the same model at 110 tokens/second on a single H100, with 19 MB proofs that can be verified in seconds. Attestable independently reports 53–77 tokens/second for a dense 31B model.
We believe that the progress should transfer to more models and architectures, yielding a flexible and powerful tool with overhead over native computation of roughly 2 orders of magnitude (about 70 to 95 times in our measurements), much less than previously expected.
Limitations
This release is a research prototype, and has the following technical limitations:
- No formal guarantees on fast executable code. We provide a Lean implementation of the protocol (including an executable “slow” Lean verifier), along with security properties proved in Lean. The paper and the fast executable code are derived from the Lean protocol, but we do not guarantee that all three (Lean, paper, code) match each other.
- The proof is about an integer model under greedy decoding. We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved. The integer version is generally expected and empirically tested to be within some small error rate of true floating-point inference generically (even taking into account non-determinism of floating-point computations), though this does not cover adversarially designed prompts.
- Architecture hiding. Our system assumes the served model uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, in which each transformer layer’s feed-forward block is replaced by multiple expert sub-networks and a router that activates only a small subset of experts for each token and our system uses the MoE structure for efficiency gains. Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model.
- Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release.
- Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens).

articles.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
articles.body:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)
Executive summary
When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.
Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:
- Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. 
  - For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.
  - Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6. Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.
- Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.
Today we are releasing five artifacts:
- The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;
- A technical report explaining the details of our system;
- A (Claude-written) protocol specification document;
- Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and
- Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.
We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.
Introduction
When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.
However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.
The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.
One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.
Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).
The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.
We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.
Trust challenges in AI proliferation
The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).
Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.
Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.
Challenge 1: pacing
Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?
How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.
Challenge 2: tamper detection
As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3
How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.
Challenge 3: text provenance
One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?
How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.
For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).
Challenge 4: model approval
Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?
How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.
A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.
Our system: FlashProve
FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.
FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:
- In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase.
- In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:
The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.
Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.
Guarantees
A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:
- A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier.
- A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.
Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.
- A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden.
- A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure.
Evaluation
We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

(For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.
- Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

- Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request.
- The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices.
Post-hoc versus in-line

Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model.
- Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release.
- Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens).

articles.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
articles.body:
In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability, which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA, Wikipedia, the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.
As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.
“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche, AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo. “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”
PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors
PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.
“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University.
“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University
Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI. Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.
Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”
To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”
AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security
After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.
“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”
This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever.
One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.”
Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.”
Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them.
Matthew Green, an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.”
In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.”
One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

articles.title: Not even $200 million could help Elon Musk buy Texas
articles.body:
James Talarico, the Democratic Texas senator-elect, not only managed to flip the state in yesterday’s midterms but prevailed in the most expensive Senate election to date. More than $573 million was spent on advertisements between Talarico, his Republican opponent Ken Paxton, and their aligned PACs. And a big chunk of that money came from just one man: Elon Musk.
Not even $200 million could help Elon Musk buy Texas
Elon Musk’s wall of money fell to the blue tsunami.
Musk reportedly spent more than $445 million supporting Republicans in the midterms, making him not only by far the biggest donor in the 2026 election cycle but also in American history. And most of his money was spent in Texas, his home state and the headquarters of both Tesla and SpaceX. Musk funneled more than $168 million to super PACs that supported Paxton; Musk’s own America PAC, to which he funneled $216 million, also spent $34.7 million of those funds in Texas. All told, that’s more than $200 million spent on a single state.
But Musk’s millions couldn’t buy him an election. Talarico beat Paxton by more than 12 points, becoming Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1988. And the governor’s seat flipped, too: Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, another beneficiary of Musk’s largesse. The Democratic fantasy of a blue Texas finally became reality — and it happened despite the efforts of the world’s first trillionaire.
More than a blue wave, the midterms were a bloodbath for Republicans, who underperformed nationally even in the states they won. Democrats’ victories across the country often came down to money. But in Texas, it didn’t happen in the way Musk hoped. Talarico framed the race as a “top versus bottom” struggle between the ultrarich and everyone else. Musk’s donations to Abbott and Paxton may have emphasized America’s wealth inequality at a time when many Americans are struggling to make ends meet under an economic crisis caused by inflation, tariffs, and the ongoing war against Iran — all the results of policy choices made by the current administration.
It’s hard to imagine just how poorly Paxton would have performed without Musk’s money. Paxton’s campaign received just $22.3 million in direct donations, a paltry sum compared with the $146 million Talarico raised from voters. Paxton got a much-needed boost from Musk, who ensured that Texans were flooded with anti-Talarico ads. Those ads, however, didn’t focus on the issues that mattered most to voters. In Texas, anti-Talarico ads largely focused on culture war issues like transgender people, a fixation of Musk’s. (Musk is estranged from his oldest daughter, who is transgender, and he has described her as having been “killed” by the “woke mind virus.”) One Facebook ad that cost between $15,000 and $20,000 urged voters to “defeat Talarico and his radical trans agenda.” According to an analysis of America PAC’s spending by 19th News, the ad was one of dozens of anti-trans ads paid for by Musk.
But Musk’s money was also a liability for Paxton, which is perhaps why the now-near-trillionaire chose to operate from behind the scenes this time around. Musk endorsed Paxton on X — claiming the “fate of Texas and America is at stake” in the election — but against all Musk’s instincts for public spectacle, he didn’t take on a surrogate role in the midterms, in Texas or elsewhere. There was no Musk-led rally, no onstage jumping, no chainsaw in sight. Instead, Talarico repeatedly emphasized the relationship between Paxton and Musk, suggesting that to vote for one man was to benefit the other. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” he said at a rally in El Paso in late October. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV screen, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black-and-white photos, that was Elon too.”
Talarico’s comments may have drawn even more attention to Musk’s cozy relationship with Paxton, which appears to be mutually beneficial. Paxton, who’s served as Texas attorney general since 2015 — aside from a brief stint in 2023 when he was impeached — has launched several investigations into organizations that criticize or antagonize Musk, according to a recent Wired report. Paxton has repeatedly followed Musk’s lead. After Musk sued the progressive media site Media Matters, Paxton investigated the publication; when Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against an advertising federation, a Paxton probe followed.
“Elon Musk wants our land,” Talarico said at his El Paso rally. “He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”
Beyond trying to buy a senator, Musk also tried to chip in for a governor. Though most of the money Musk spent in Texas went to Paxton, he also threw a few million to Abbott, with whom he also has a close relationship — so much so that Hinojosa sued to view all 1,400 pages of correspondence between the two. And Musk wasn’t the only tech executive to support Abbott. The Republican, who promised to make Texas the “epicenter” of AI development, also received $300,000 from Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown, as well as funds from several data center developers.
Musk seems to sense that the political winds have shifted. Usually a prolific poster, Musk deleted a “Vote red early!” post from Election Day and barely had anything to say on X that night aside from a quip about putting data centers in space. The other states he threw money at hardly fared better. Democrats won in Ohio, where Musk’s America PAC spent $10.4 million, and Michigan, where he spent $9.8 million. The Republican party’s only real victory was in Florida, and they barely managed to eke out a victory there.
The amount of money Musk spent on this election cycle is both staggering and unprecedented — and it’s also meaningless to him. Musk lost half a billion dollars in his failed bid to buy the midterms, an amount that adds up to less than half a percent of his net worth. It’s possible that his loss will signal that even the world’s richest man can’t bend the electorate to his will. But it’s just as likely that he’ll spend even more money next time.

articles.title: Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers
articles.body:
Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers (arstechnica.com) 41
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: [S]tate-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage.
On November 2, Putin also signed a decree ordering Russian data center operators to set aside 10 percent of available space and capacity in case the Russian government requires it, according to independent Russian news publication Meduza. That may indicate growing Kremlin concerns about the vulnerability of Russian cloud computing infrastructure during its war with Ukraine. Putin's decree also allows a special Russian government commission to authorize use of foreign data centers in consultation with Russia's Federal Security Service. That marks a notable policy change because Putin and the Russian parliament previously enacted Russia's "Sovereign Internet Law," which has blocked Russian companies from using cloud computing infrastructure outside Russia's borders.
Russia's push for a sovereign and increasingly closed Internet has resulted in a highly centralized system under a few Russian tech companies like Yandex. That hyper-centralized system has now proven vulnerable during wartime, as Ukrainian drone strikes on key Russian data centers created widespread disruptions for popular payment and digital banking apps, e-commerce platforms, video streaming services, and ride-hailing and food delivery apps, among others. Yandex has also been forced to relocate all three of its main supercomputers after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted the AI data centers where they were originally housed, Meduza reported.

articles.title: Kitty 0.50
articles.body:
Changelog¶
kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast, GPU based terminal. To update kitty, follow the instructions.
Recent major new features¶
Docked windows [0.50]¶
kitty windows can now be docked to an edge of another window or
of the tab. Docked windows are placed outside the layout, making them perfect
for status bars, file trees or a shell kept next to your editor. A dock
attached to a window follows it around, moving with it to other tabs and closing
when it closes. Create docks with launch --type=window-dock or
launch --type=tab-dock. Docks are saved in sessions too.
Restore after logout [0.50]¶
Like other applications, kitty can now save its state when you log out, restart or
shut down your computer, and restore it the next time it starts. Simply set
restore_session_after_logout and every kitty instance comes back with all
its OS Windows, tabs and windows in place, including their scrollback. On
macOS, the saved state is encrypted using a key stored in your keychain. See
Restoring kitty after logging out for details.
Custom shaders [0.49]¶
kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders. These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised.
See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty.
Performance improvements [0.49]¶
This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details:
- Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to
- Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths
- Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+).
- Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters
- Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD, filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images
- Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives.
- Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped
Vertical tabs [0.48]¶
kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows.
Drag and drop for terminal programs [0.47]¶
kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program.
Mousing [0.46]¶
kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next
level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for smooth scrolling and momentum based scrolling
for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience.
Additionally, you can now drag kitty tabs around with the mouse
to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into
their own OS Window.
Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented.
Choose files, fast [0.45]¶
A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text.
On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs.
Sessions [0.43]¶
kitty has long had support for Sessions, aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file, for seamless and intuitive session file creation.
A scrollbar for the kitty scrollback [0.43]¶
A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar
that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear
automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is extensively
configurable in kitty.conf. Note that the old scrollback_indicator_opacity
option is deprecated.
Multiple cursors [0.43]¶
kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last.
Access kitty with a single keypress [0.42]¶
kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress.
See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up.
Multiple sized text [0.40]¶
kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol.
Cursor trails [0.37]¶
Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy
to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but
works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull
request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be
turned on by the cursor_trail option in kitty.conf.
Variable font support [0.36]¶
Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text
rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports
OpenType Variable fonts.
These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and
spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with
support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will
look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization
abilities, such as: symbol_map, text_composition_strategy,
font_features and modify_font. kitty knows text rendering is
important, and goes the extra mile for it.
Desktop notifications [0.36]¶
kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features.
Wayland goodies [0.34]¶
Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements:
- Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background
- Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol
- The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically
- kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor
With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor.

of each marker to the next one (#10591)

0.40.1 [2025-03-18]¶

Window visibility instead of focus state when set to invisible on
