US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats win Senate control and edge
articles.body:
This live blog is now closed. You can follow our latest midterms election coverage here:
History made in races across the US – as it happened
Democrats flip Senate seats in Texas, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Ohio; voters reject Trump’s agenda in ‘blue wave’
Wed 4 Nov 2026 07.24 EST
First published on Tue 3 Nov 2026 17.49 EST
Wed 4 Nov 2026 07.24 EST
First published on Tue 3 Nov 2026 17.49 EST
Summary of midterm results so far
The Democratic party has taken control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump and Republicans. Here are some of the key results, historic victories and political developments from the midterm elections so far:
- The Democrats have secured 228 seats in the House (with 218 needed for a majority) and 54 seats in the Senate (with 51 needed for control). The party has flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds, including Kansas – which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century – Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In the House, the Democrats have flipped more than two dozen districts.
- History was made in Michigan as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Republican Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed said in his election night speech.
- Other seismic wins in federal and state races for the Democrats include James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton, who is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; and progressive Troy Jackson, who unseated Susan Collins in Maine, ending her 30-year career in the US Senate.
- Democrat Aaron Ford won the race for governor in Nevada, toppling Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first black governor.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”
- Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” he said.
Read our full report here:
Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.
“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.
He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.
Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.
If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.
“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Read more:
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.
Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.
Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.
In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.
But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
Read more:
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
 Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.
These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Democrat Tina Kotek wins re-election for governor in Oregon
The incumbent Democratic governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, has won her re-election bid against Republican Christine Drazan.
It is the second time Kotek has defeated Drazan, after the two faced off in the 2022 governor race.
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
The Democrat’s faith was weaponised throughout the race, with Trump calling him a “jihadist” and Rogers questioning his loyalty to the US. El-Sayed met the attacks with defiance, telling Trump that he could “just go on and call me senator after November”.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
 My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”
My colleague Joseph Gedeon has more:
Latest midterm results - at a glance
It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.
- Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.
- There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.
- We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.
- Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races. Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Democrat Tina Kotek wins re-election for governor in Oregon
The incumbent Democratic governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, has won her re-election bid against Republican Christine Drazan.
It is the second time Kotek has defeated Drazan, after the two faced off in the 2022 governor race.
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
The Democrat’s faith was weaponised throughout the race, with Trump calling him a “jihadist” and Rogers questioning his loyalty to the US. El-Sayed met the attacks with defiance, telling Trump that he could “just go on and call me senator after November”.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
 My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”
My colleague Joseph Gedeon has more:
Latest midterm results - at a glance
It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.
- Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.
- There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.
- We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.
- Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races. Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

articles.title: From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region
articles.body:
From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region
By Krishna Ramanujan, Cornell Chronicle
Scientists studying the neurology of tame foxes identified changes in a part of the brain that has previously been associated with aggression, according to a new paper that compared the brains of domesticated, aggressive and wild foxes.
The changes occurred in an area at the base of the brain called ventromedial hypothalamus, which is known to drive aggression, control decisions related to energy use and is important for maternal instincts and social behaviors in mice.
The study, published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology, takes advantage of a classic experiment that started in Siberia in the late 1950s where Russian geneticists noticed some foxes on silver fox farms were friendlier toward human caretakers while others were more aggressive.
They then selectively bred friendlier foxes with each other and after only six generations of this selection, they had litters of puppies that interacted with humans. The cuddlier foxes also had physical features characteristic of animal domestication, including floppy ears and shorter snouts.
“We wanted to understand, what are the neurological underpinnings of these changes in behaviors that occurred very rapidly with this selection,” said Eirene Markenscoff-Papadimitriou, assistant professor of molecular biology and genetics in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS), a Rita Allen Foundation Scholar and the paper’s senior author.
The research has implications for how environmental pressures of all kinds can alter brain structure on short timescales, Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said.
In the study, the authors decided to focus on the ventromedial hypothalamus because previous research had already identified different cell types there that control aggression in mice.
Working with Russian fox colony scientists, the study’s authors received a shipment of nine silver fox brains: three from foxes bred to be tame, three from foxes similarly bred for aggressive traits and three wild foxes. The brains were preserved and very thinly sliced. In the ventromedial hypothalamus, a fluorescent RNA scope allowed them identify markers for different cell types there.
Previously, other scientists had employed a technique called optogenetics in experiments with mice where light was used to activate specific neurons that express a receptor protein called estrogen receptor alpha in the ventromedial hypothalamus.
“If you activate them, the mouse will immediately attack another mouse,” Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said. “We hypothesized that there would be differences in the abundance of this particular cell type, and we did find that the tame fox hypothalamus had fewer of these estrogen receptor expressing neurons, which are known to be part of the aggression circuit,” she said.
Now that the paper’s authors observed this difference, next steps will involve trying to understand why domestication leads to these changes in the ventromedial hypothalamus, a brain area has not been well studied before this work.
Study co-author Anna Kukekova, an associate professor of genomic biology and animal sciences at the University of Illinois-Urbana-Champaign, may explore how mutations in different parts of the fox genome affect the development of these particular neurons.
Jared Klein ‘25, a former research technician in Markenscoff-Papadimitriou’s lab, is the paper’s first author. Co-authors include Andrew Miller, professor of population medicine and diagnostic sciences in the College of Veterinary Medicine; and Anastasiya Kharlamova, Anastasiya Vladirimova and Darya Shepeleva at the Institute of Cytology and Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
The study was funded by Cornell’s Center for Vertebrate Genomics.

Adam Allington

articles.title: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.body:
Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry.
Data centers lost the midterms
In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.
Data centers lost the midterms
In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.
Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures. And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development.
It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place.
Ballot measures
Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to a site compiled by Redbud Consulting, the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The Town of Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The City of El Dorado, Kansas, voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years.
Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development
Texas
Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a statewide moratorium on data center development, while Abbott took a more measured approach. He announced a new audit this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has previously praised data center expansion in the state.
In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers.
Florida
Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate.
Pennsylvania
Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro signed an executive order that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she supports a development pause of up to three years.
Ohio
Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a leaked memo that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier helped install data center tax breaks as lieutenant governor, though he more recently introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone as far as to call for a moratorium, he’s said that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input.
Republicans warned that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates
Michigan
Democrat and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race over Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was one of the earliest politicians to stake his position on data centers, and has called for a pause on new developments “until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers called for a one-year state moratorium this summer, but not a federal ban.
As of Wednesday morning, NBC News had not yet called a House race between Democratic organizer William Lawrence and Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, but Lawrence held a lead with 92 percent of the vote in. Similar to El-Sayed, Lawrence stated his position on data centers early on, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new developments during his primary campaign. Barrett introduced legislation this summer to bar nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and give locals more control.
Maine
Democrat and former Maine State Senator Troy Jackson ousted Republican Sen. Susan Collins from her Senate seat. The state legislature passed what would have been the country’s first moratorium on data centers, had the governor not vetoed it. But polls show that opposition to data centers among Maine residents remained strong. Jackson supported a state moratorium on data centers, while Collins opposed such a measure but called for more local control and protection for energy ratepayers.
Wisconsin
Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won the governor’s race over Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. Neither Crowley nor Tiffany favored a moratorium on data centers, and have distanced themselves from previous support. Crowley won his primary over progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong, who supported a moratorium. Both Crowley and Tiffany said they wanted to end state tax subsidies for data centers though they’ve accused one another of flip-flopping their stances.
Nevada
Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford successfully flipped the governor’s seat from incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo, whom he’d branded “data center Joe.” Lombardo has previously made supportive comments about data centers, but more recently introduced an executive order making tax incentives contingent on data centers covering power costs and meeting certain environmental standards. Ford previously championed a 2015 data center tax-break bill, but said today’s data centers are different from those years ago, and now supports a pause on all tax breaks for new data centers.
Georgia
Democrat and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governor’s seat over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Bottoms favored a moratorium on data centers to review environmental and cost effects, while Jackson preferred to leave decisions up to locals.
Arizona
Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs fought off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Both opposed a moratorium on data centers in favor of power and water use standards.
Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes held onto her seat over a challenge from Republican state legislator Warren Petersen. Mayes took a more hardline view than her Democratic peer, Hobbs, by endorsing a state moratorium on data center development. Petersen opposed a moratorium, and said data centers are necessary for technology residents use every day.
Iowa
Democratic state auditor Rob Sand won the governor’s seat over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand did not support a data center moratorium, which Lahn did. But both agreed on ending tax breaks for the developments.
South Carolina
Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina’s Senate seat blue in a race against Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who had taken over the seat after her brother Lindsey Graham died. Andrews supported a two-year data center moratorium, while Graham opposed a pause and got significant support from a super PAC allied with the data center industry.

articles.title: YC's Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
articles.body:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.
On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.
“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.
He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”
As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.
For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”
Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.
“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”
But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

articles.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
articles.body:
Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino (
https://kino.ai
). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at 
https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video
 and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at 
https://kino.ai/launch-video
Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack.
Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match.
Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way.
To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny.
I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America (https://regressions.net). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet.
Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing.
Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing.
We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything.
The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai. We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now.
If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

articles.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
articles.body:
AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections
AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.
As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.
AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.
Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue
AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.
The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.
AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.
"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops
AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.
Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.
Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.
"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."
AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.
Embedded business strong, set to accelerate
As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.
AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.
"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."
Beating Intel
For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.
In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.
If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.
The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
articles.body:
AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections
AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.
As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.
AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.
Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue
AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.
The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.
AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.
"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops
AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.
Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.
Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.
"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."
AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.
Embedded business strong, set to accelerate
As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.
AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.
"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."
Beating Intel
For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.
In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.
If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.
The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
articles.body:
Letting users trust their own MCP clients, without opening a phishing hole
The problem
You run your own agent: a Slack bot, a service on a VPS, an MCP client you wrote over a weekend. You want it on your files, which on Stream Vessel means your own S3 bucket, where an agent can read, write and delete through the MCP server. The agent speaks MCP’s standard OAuth sign-in: it registers itself, opens a browser, you click Approve, it gets a token.
It fails at step one. At registration the agent named its redirect URI, the address your browser returns to after you approve, carrying a one-time authorization code the agent swaps for a token. Yours is https://agent.yourhost.example/callback; the answer is invalid_redirect_uri. The server only accepts addresses on its operator’s allowlist: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and a few others. Getting yours added means asking the operator to change a config file.
The server cannot simply accept any address. That list is the addresses the post office will deliver your house keys to. Without it, a stranger registers a fake “Claude” that has the keys sent to their place, and phishes your storage with one link. So the server is either closed to you or unsafe for everyone.
Both failures are common. On the closed side, this is what people run into:
“The redirect URI is not allowed, the URL is not part of Atlassian whitelisted domains for registered MCP Clients.” — an error users, Cursor’s among them, reported in the Atlassian developer community
“…each host application must have a registered GitHub App (or OAuth App) to authenticate on behalf of the user.” — GitHub MCP server, policies and governance; otherwise you fall back to a personal access token
On the open side, a May 2026 study that tested 119 OAuth-enabled MCP servers found registration endpoints on 114 of them, 95.8%, that
“accept arbitrary redirect_uri values from anonymous requesters.”
The attack: one link, one click, someone else’s bucket
Say your server accepts any registration and any redirect address. An attacker with no account on it can take over a user’s access in four steps:
- Register a client named “Claude” whose redirect URI is https://evil.example/cb. Open registration is anonymous, by design.
- Send a signed-in user a normal-looking /oauth/authorize link: “Reconnect your storage to Claude”.
- The user sees your real consent screen, on your real domain, in their real session, and clicks Approve.
- The code lands at evil.example. The attacker trades it for a token and is now the user.
PKCE does not help: it lets only the client that started a flow finish it, and the attacker started this one. The client name is self-declared and proves nothing. The consent screen shows the redirect host, but claude-connect.app passes a glance. It is the same trick as the fake-app approval prompts sent to Microsoft 365 users: a real page and a real Approve; there the attacker uses an app the platform registered, here an address the server should never have accepted.
The user does approve, but on false information. A redirect allowlist is what makes an approval mean what the user thinks it means: whatever the name says, the keys can only go where the list says.
This is not hypothetical. In January 2026 Obsidian Security reported this chain against Square’s MCP server: self-registration accepted any redirect address, and one click exposed a merchant’s profile, transactions and bank details. In the researchers’ words, “any user who had previously authorized the Square MCP server was vulnerable.” Square’s fix, they note, only applied to newly registered clients.
Others found the same chain on an MCP proxy in front of a company’s single sign-on, worth a 24-hour access token and a 14-day refresh token per click, and across bug-bounty programs, where it was sometimes waved off as social engineering. SickSec’s answer: the victim never leaves the trusted domain.
A quieter problem rides along. When a request fails a check after its redirect address was accepted, the error is sent to that address. So a server that accepts any address is an open redirector on its own domain: a crafted authorize link with a bad scope bounces visitors to any site, under your hostname. RFC 9700 describes exactly this case.
What the spec says, and what servers actually do
The MCP spec names the risk and leaves the policy to each server. Its security considerations say authorization servers MUST validate exact redirect URIs, SHOULD only redirect automatically to a URI they trust, and MAY instead inform the user and let them decide. The last two are RFC 9700’s sentences, word for word. What “trust” means is left open.
Registration is shifting too. The 2026-07-28 client registration page deprecates Dynamic Client Registration (a client registering itself over an API, no human involved) for Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), where the client id is an HTTPS URL to a document listing its redirect URIs. CIMD says who publishes a client, not whether this user meant to connect it.
The OAuth working group has been here. In a December 2025 thread on the IETF OAuth list, Warren Parad argued that unauthenticated registration turns an MCP authorization server into an open redirector. Aaron Parecki’s quoted reply points to RFC 9700 §4.11.2, which starts from exactly that setup.
In practice, servers sit at one of two poles:
Loopback means localhost or 127.0.0.1: an app on the user’s own machine, waiting for the browser to come back.
The first pole costs real users, and clients will not fix it for you. A Claude Code issue from June 2026 reports that organizations with exact-match redirect allowlists cannot sign in from Claude Code, because its http://localhost:<port>/callback host and path are fixed. It was closed as not planned in July 2026. The server has to move.
This is not a new idea
Letting users vouch for their own app’s callback is old. GitHub has developers create an OAuth app and type in its callback URL. The MCP spec’s pre-registration option describes a server page where users register a client by hand. And an organization can add trusted redirect domains to Atlassian’s MCP server. None of these fit a client that registers itself anonymously: the first two need a client id made somewhere else, and Atlassian decides for a whole organization. So we kept self-registration and let each user decide at sign-in, for their own account, beside the server-wide list.
Our design: trust is per user, decided at sign-in
We keep the operator’s allowlist and loopback for local clients, unchanged and open to every account. On top of it, each user can trust a handful of exact https redirect addresses for their own account; ours caps at 10. On Stream Vessel that is “Trusted app addresses” on the MCP page of the web app.
The key move is when the check runs. Registration happens before anyone signs in, so it cannot know whose list to consult. So registration accepts any https URI, and the decision waits for the authorize page, where the user is known:
One rule sits under every branch: no code and no error is ever redirected to an address unless every account or this user trusts it. Before sign-in no user’s list applies, so even the OAuth library’s own validation errors (a bad PKCE challenge, an unknown scope) wait for sign-in, and a refusal is a page on our host. That closes the open-redirect hole along with the phishing one, and it covers the Deny button too: n8n’s CVE-2026-42230 (April 2026) sent users who denied consent straight to an attacker’s registered address.
Seven ways around it, each closed
Most of these rules came from trying to break the first version.
- Only the user’s own browser session changes the list, never an app or API token, so a stolen token cannot widen where the user’s codes may go.
- Adding from the refusal page means typing the host. The page shows the host, the full address as plain text (never a link), the account it would join, and a warning: if someone sent you this link, close the page. “Trust and continue” stays disabled until the host is typed, so one click from a phishing email is not enough.
- The consent screen names this sign-in’s redirect, and why it is allowed. A client can register several addresses at once, so it could list claude.ai beside its own. The screen shows only the one this sign-in returns to, and its basis: on the allowlist, loopback, or “you trusted this address yourself on 3 Nov 2026”. The spec requires showing the host for metadata-document clients, though the May 2026 study found 60.5% of tested servers don’t; the basis is what makes it mean something.
- Every addition is emailed, and audited while the activity log is on. The email leads with the host, says when and to which account, and keeps the full address from turning into a link. It is the signal a phished user would otherwise never get.
- Removing an address cuts the app off, even mid-sign-in. It revokes every grant (an approval the user gave) through that address and drops codes approved but not yet exchanged. A code lives about a minute; without this, a code in flight becomes a grant after the removal.
- Hosts the browser and the server read differently are refused. A URI parser may keep good.example%2eevil.example as one literal host while the browser goes to good.example.evil.example. A page that names one host and sends the user to another defeats the typed-host check, so such hosts are refused at registration and on the list.
- Exact match only. No wildcards, no prefix match, no loopback-style port flexibility.
What it does not stop, and what we turned down
It does not stop a determined social engineer: a user talked into typing an attacker’s host and approving is phished, whichever tier they pick. We bound it rather than prevent it: the typed host, the warnings, the email, instant disconnection on removal, and a consent screen that starts at read-only and says the user trusted the address.
We first capped user-trusted addresses at write access, so a phished grant could change data but not delete it. We dropped the cap: users connecting their own agents wanted full access, and the cap was a backstop, not the defense.
Beyond the two poles above, we weighed:
A checklist for your own MCP server
- Decide where codes may go at authorize, with the signed-in user known, not at registration.
- Check every answer, errors included, against that rule before redirecting, and refuse to a page on your own host. Do it at authorize, not only at token exchange: Cloudflare’s workers-oauth-provider shipped CVE-2025-4143 in May 2025 for checking only the latter.
- Show the redirect host of this request on the consent screen, and say why it is allowed.
- Make widening the list a deliberate act outside the sign-in flow, or behind a typed confirmation.
- Email the user every time an address is added.
- Make removal revoke grants and in-flight codes.
- Refuse URIs whose host the browser and your parser read differently.
Want to try it? In your own agent, add Stream Vessel’s MCP server, https://mcp.streamvessel.com, and sign in. If your agent isn’t on our list, you’ll land on the refusal page shown above, where you can trust its address and carry on.

articles.title: Coffee's new status symbol is a machine without plastic
articles.body:
For decades, it was all the bells and whistles that was the selling point for a fancy coffee machine. Now, consumers are looking for what it lacks.
Growing concern over microplastics and sustainability is sparking a wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines.
Coffee companies and appliance makers have released new machines and redesigned capsules in recent months. Keurig and Lavazza’s new pods ditch the traditional plastic cups for compostable coffee tablets. Caraway’s new machine uses traditional coffee grounds, but unlike a conventional drip machine, the stainless steel and glass machine doesn’t have plastic in its brew path.
More research is needed to determine the actual harm microplastics cause. But nine in 10 Americans are concerned about the effect of the minuscule plastic pieces on the planet and their bodies, according to a 2025 poll conducted by environmental group 5 Gyres; and studies have shown that pods shed microplastics.
The growth in pricey equipment and plastic-free pods fits a broader pattern of consumers trading up on home coffee equipment since the pandemic, said Peter Giuliano, senior adviser for research at Specialty Coffee Association.
The appeal and growth combine three things: health worries about microplastics, concern about plastic in the environment and the “feeling that metal and glass are more ‘luxury’ than plastic,” he told CNN.
New pods
In June, Lavazza introduced Tablì in the US, a $129 machine that uses only single-serve espresso tablets made with compressed ground coffee — a shift from its capsules made from plastic and aluminum.
The tablets are made by a custom technology that “compresses precisely dosed, ground, and tamped coffee into a solid, ready-to-use tab,” Lavazza said in a press release.
The Italian company says the new machine is its “largest investment yet” in the United States as it looks to double revenue to $1 billion by 2029, unlocking the stranglehold Keurig Dr. Pepper has on the coffee market.
Tablì is aimed at customers who want a sustainable alternative to the traditional pod, according to Daniele Foti, vice president of marketing for Lavazza North America.
“Consumers want to enjoy their coffee without the waste that usually comes with single-serve,” he told CNN.
Keurig, which ushered in the boom of plastics with their K-Cups back in the 1990s, launched in October a new line of compostable pods with a specially designed machine called the Alta. (The new pods don’t fit in the old machines.)
Called AltaRounds, the pods have been in development since 2020 in response to consumers’ shifting sustainability and health preferences.
The new pods represent a “significant reduction in plastic compared to our K-Cup pods,” said Phil Drapeau, senior vice president for Keurig’s Future Coffee Systems unit.
“We’ve heard clearly from customers that they want more sustainable products and specifically less plastic and plastic waste,” Drapeau told CNN. “Our data shows that drink variety, quality, and less plastic waste are high priorities across almost every group.”
Keurig has come under fire in the past over its pods, agreeing in 2022 to pay $10 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it misled consumers by marketing its plastic K-Cups as recyclable, though it denied any wrongdoing.
But while the pods and the machine contain less plastic, they are considerably more expensive than a traditional Keurig machine. The Alta bundle that includes glassware and pods costs $499.
Melissa Valliant, director of communications for 5 Gyres, said that both the Lavazza and Keurig products still use plastic packaging, which “ends up in a landfill, incinerator, or our environment after use, contributing to the planet’s growing plastic pollution crisis.”
New machine
Caraway has focused on developing a $495 coffee machine, released last month, that’s created entirely of stainless steel and glass, ensuring that no plastic touches the ground coffee. (Lavazza’s and Keurig’s machines contain some amounts of plastic.)
Developing a coffee machine with plastic-free brew path was challenging, according to Caraway CEO Jordan Nathan. That’s because the pricey glass and steel parts all need to be custom-made.
“We had to make the best coffee possible with no plastic on the interior with a full metal body, but also in a small (counter) footprint that had a single dial,” he told CNN.
Concern over plastic in the kitchen and its affects on the endocrine system has been growing for the past few years, Nathan said, referencing a viral article that linked black plastics in the kitchen to alarming levels of toxic flame retardants.
Social media, influencers and various scientific studies have all fueled the conversation, with parents and other health-conscious shoppers avoiding plastic where they can, including in makeup, food and bedding. Caraway’s other plastic-free products, like cutting boards, have soared in sales over the past three years.
Coffee is a natural next step, Nathan added, because “you never want to heat plastic.”
Demand for Caraway’s new 10-cup coffee maker has been so strong that it’s sold out until January, forcing the company to ramp up production. Meanwhile, Keurig and Lavazza reported similar interest with both company’s product selling out quickly after their initial release.
That appetite for these pods and machines signals the industry will move toward more plastic-free alternatives, Nathan said.
“If you’re not doing it, you’re behind where the puck is moving,” he concluded.

articles.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
articles.body:
Study reveals distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in younger patients
Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.
In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.
"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."
"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."
The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older. Using a technique called single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the researchers measured gene activity in more than 850,000 cancer cells and other cells in the tumors. The technique, which works with frozen tissue, enabled the team to build a detailed map of tumor cells by studying archived samples with extensive clinical record data.
Rather than dividing the tumor samples into two data sets and comparing the younger and older age groups, the researchers looked for factors that changed gradually with age, accounting for tumor location, stage, sex, and prior treatment in their analyses. This approach revealed subtle differences that likely would have been obscured by a simple two-data set comparison.
Among tumors of the most common colorectal cancer subtype, younger patients’ tumors had a significantly higher proportion of connective and supporting cells relative to cancer cells. A higher proportion of connective and supporting cells has been linked to chemotherapy resistance in several types of solid cancer. The team confirmed this pattern using gene-activity data from 564 other tumors and computer analysis of stained tissue images from another 712 tumors.
Younger patients also had higher activity of long non-coding RNAs, molecules that can regulate genes without making proteins. Some appeared repeatedly across different types of cancer cells. Many are "dark" RNAs, whose functions remain largely unknown. The team also saw gene activity suggesting stronger signaling between cells that can help cancer cells move and invade nearby tissue in younger patients.
"Our study is an advance from previous work in that we analyzed tumors from a large number of patients and used single-cell approaches to find novel features unique to tumors from young patients," said Xavier, a co-senior author of the study, a core institute member at the Broad Institute, Kurt Isselbacher Professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and Vice Director of the Gene Lay Institute. Xavier is also a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham. "This work sets the stage for future mechanistic studies on how these cell programs interact with chemicals from the diet and from gut microbes to cause early-onset colorectal cancer."
Although the findings provide key insight into colorectal cancer in young individuals, they do not yet provide proof that these differences cause more aggressive disease. One remaining question is whether there are differences in immune responses in these tumors across ages — the researchers' methods captured relatively few immune cells. Future studies will explore how these changes may affect cancer growth and spread, and whether they offer opportunities for prevention or treatment.

articles.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
articles.body:
Study reveals distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in younger patients
Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.
In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.
"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."
"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."
The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older.
