articles.title: Assyria is Far from Ancient in Esther Elia’s Characterizations of Contemporary ‘Diasporic Deities’
articles.body:
Assyria is Far from Ancient in Esther Elia’s Characterizations of Contemporary ‘Diasporic Deities’
Across ancient Mesopotamia, lamassu figures assumed the form of a winged goddess. In the ancient Assyrian Empire, giant bulls or lions with human heads and wings represented the deities, which artisans often carved at a monumental scale to protect cities and palaces. For Albuquerque-based Esther Elia, who is of Assyrian and Irish descent, lamassu are anything but a relic of the distant past. Through sculpture, paintings, and textiles, the artist explores contemporary Assyrian experience through pattern, fashion, and autobiography.
Her solo exhibition, Bazaar Ashuraya at Hecho a Mano, centers around a new collection of acrylic paintings, plus tile mosaics and functional objects. Elia delves into the theme of home, where lamps, garments, and paintings evocative of rugs or tapestries portray vibrant figures, shapes, and objects associated with daily life. Compositions such as “Sharrat Wearing Adidas” and “Esther and Zahra Wearing Farm Rio” playfully nod to contemporary fashion and folk designs.
“The home is where Assyria lives and breathes,” Elia says in a statement. She adds:
The home is where our language is spoken. Even if we speak English or Arabic or Farsi or French or Swedish outside of the home, the home is where Assyrian food is made, where Assyrian customs thrive, and where culture is maintained as well as created—pushed forward. As we mix with diaspora, our clothes, furnishings, and habits reflect the mixing with these new places.
Elia’s sculptures have reached nearly life-size through the use of Mexican tiles on cement board and plywood, with wheels affixed to the bases so they can move around. She coined these her “diasporic deities” because they incorporate materials readily sourced in the Southwest and are designed to be adaptable to different spaces.
Bazaar Ashuraya runs from November 6 to 29 in Santa Fe, and the artist was recently announced as a 2027 resident of the John Michael Kohler Art Center and Kohler Co.’s Arts/Industry program. See more on Elia’s Instagram.

articles.title: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.body:
People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.
Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”
“What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds, on top of its existing steep commitments. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds, for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them.
The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion.
I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds, meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt.
It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal, is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.
This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

articles.title: 'It's just vape, nail, charity shops': Can anything save UK high street?
articles.body:
On 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.
Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.
Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks. Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13%, reports Savills.
Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”
Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.
A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant, far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.
The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “disembowel towns and villages” and disadvantage those unable to drive.
Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.
The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. Recent police data shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre recorded 836 crimes in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”
For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.
Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.
Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”
The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: research by the thinktank Power to Change published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”
The town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.
Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?
She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.
The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.
London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. The indoor shopping centre opened the year after Thatcher’s ascendancy to leader of the opposition in 1975. Already there was consensus among local authorities that out-of-town shopping centres would destroy high streets but, after the Tories entered Downing Street in 1979, planning rules were eased. “There is a change of attitude in the 1980s which begins to allow these out-of-town locations,” says Alistair Kefford, the chair of urban studies at Leiden University in the Netherlands. In 1981, there was one out-of-town retail park in the UK. By 1988, there were 90 and at the end of 1996, there were 385.
In the end, the critics were right. “There’s only a certain level of consumer demand within a regional economy,” says Kefford. “If you build a wonderful, shiny, exciting new shopping mall or retail park, it doesn’t create a lot of new shoppers. They just stop going somewhere else.”
The bruising figures bear this out. In 2024, 13,479 shops across the UK closed their doors. While retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a tenth of employment, an area’s former glory is often starkly highlighted by its decrepit high street. “Dying high streets make people feel ashamed of their place, that their life is falling apart,” says Eddie Blake, a director at the architecture practice Studio Weave.
How to save the high street has become fertile political territory. Parkgate lies within John Healey’s constituency. In 2019, the now-chancellor scolded M&S for shutting its branch in the shopping complex, about a decade after relocating from Rotherham town centre, meaning the retailer would “disappear from the town for the first time in 125 years”. Since entering No 11, Healey has said “blighted” high streets will soon be “on the up”. Last month, Andy Burnham announced £210m in funding to regenerate down-on-their-luck high streets. But Kefford is sceptical. “Retail is a barometer – it’s not an engine. Where you see retail doing well, it’s a sign that the regional economy itself is doing well, but retail by itself won’t make a place wealthy. It’s not an engine of growth because it relies on people spending their disposable income,” he says.
Efforts to turn the ship can often be futile. “Once a location has set off down a particular path, it’s very hard to get out of it. In fact, everything leads further and further down that path. The narrowing range of shops, the growth of empty properties – these are things that snowball and get worse and worse,” says Kefford.
So, are UK high streets doomed? Shops “are probably not going to come back”, says Kefford, but there’s still hope. “In the 1950s and 1960s, town centres sustained loads of uses. There were many more houses and social activities: churches, working men’s clubs, community associations, charities, theatres. We need to think more fundamentally and creatively about what is the point of a town centre,” he says.
This may be good for society, too. Blake says the retail parks and shopping centres, and the cars we use to get to them, contribute to an “atomised culture that makes people feel alone”. A multifunction high street can better facilitate social interaction: “The small-grain interactions of social life are better, higher quality, and more frequent.”
Until then, many of us will be drawn to these bland, uninspiring shopping pens on the fringes of town. On my way to the train station, the No 8 bus pulls up on the high street, having just stopped at Parkgate. Sure enough, the passengers who alight are carrying bags from Primark, TK Maxx and Sports Direct.

articles.title: Kemi Badenoch says Africans should apologise for slavery
articles.body:
Despite reports that the UK attempted to keep reparations off the formal agenda for the Commonwealth summit attended by King Charles and the UK prime minister, they are in the air. British Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch is among those detractors who have argued that it is African nations who should apologise for the transatlantic slave trade. It may seem like a spectacular case of whataboutery (it is) but it also touches on an enduring tension in some Black communities surrounding African involvement in capturing and enslaving people. This week, I speak to two historians to sort fact from fiction.
When discussing slavery, we should be “honest about the whole history”, Kemi Badenoch wrote in a recent post on X. Her statement comes after months of mounting pressure on Britain’s monarchy and politicians to formally apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, and offer reparations to affected Caribbean nations. Badenoch continued: “If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?”
While the question was asked in bad faith, many within Black communities are unable to confidently answer it. In conversations with African and Caribbean colleagues at the Guardian, plenty of us experience division within our communities around the subject of African people’s participation in enslavement. The topic can be incredibly sensitive and difficult to tackle without a firm grounding in the history and political economy of the transatlantic slave trade. Yet, the experts I spoke to made it clear why African nations should not be held to the same standard as European countries and the US when atoning for their historical crimes.
Slavery was a system created by Europe and the US
Writer and historian Panashe Chigumadzi says that in understanding enslavement and who should be held to account, it is crucial that we see it as a system. Chigumadzi – who was the architect of the continental African Union’s landmark reparations framework – tells me that the trade was a structure that legally positioned all Black people as enslaveable property. No one was safe from this, whether on the continent or in the diaspora, king or commoner. She says: “[Badenoch] assumes Africans are ‘co-defendants’ and not ‘co-plaintiffs’ in prosecuting the case for a crime that fundamentally restructured the world as we know it, and created what we now know as the modern world racial capitalist system.”
Bayo Holsey, an associate professor of African American studies who specialises in west Africa at Emory University, agrees. She emphasises the overarching system that created a slave economy: the colonisation of the Caribbean and the Americas. “Europeans created the demand for enslaved labour,” the academic tells me. “The Atlantic slave trade would not have existed without this demand.”
In the latter part of the 17th century, demand for African captives on plantations had grown so much that capturing enslaved people was only possible through raiding and warfare. Given this, UK reparations would not only help repair the harm that the descendants of enslaved people have inherited, but would redress what Holsey describes as “the ill-gotten wealth of western nations”.
African people were victims of enslavement, too
We must also look at present day wealth – the economic growth of many European nations and the US was facilitated by enslavement. “The slave trade shaped the economic advantages that these countries enjoy today,” Holsey tells me. The case is fundamentally not the same in Africa. “Much of the wealth that select African individuals gained from the slave trade evaporated with the onset of colonial rule,” she says.
Africa was victimised by the slave trade too. Holsey tells me that while a small number of African people engaged in slave trading and accrued wealth, many more were victims of the trade. “They experienced fear, social instability, and the loss of loved ones as a result,” she says. Estimates based on the Slave Voyages database suggest that approximately 12.5 million enslaved Africans were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas, of whom 10.7 million survived the crossing. These figures exclude those who died before embarkation.
This depopulation destabilised the west and west-central coasts of the continent, devastating entire societies. Chigumadzi argues that the “scramble for Africa” in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the continent was invaded, divided and colonised, was a “structural continuation of the original crime of racialised chattel enslavement”.
Holsey tells me: “Today, most African nations face economic precarity as a result of historical and present-day inequities within the global economic order”. “So, unlike European nations and the US, African nations do not enjoy ongoing benefits from past participation in the slave trade. Therefore, they should not be targeted to repair the harm done by this vile system.”
Many African nations have made efforts towards repair
“Britain has already paid reparations for racialised chattel enslavement,” Chigumadzi says. “It paid them to the enslavers.” After the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, the British government agreed to pay 40% of the national budget in compensation to 46,000 enslavers, a sum that wasn’t paid off until 2015.
Passing the buck to African nations ignores the fact that many have attempted to meaningfully address their role in slavery and its ongoing legacy. In recent decades, leaders from Libya, Nigeria, Benin, Ghana, Cameroon and Uganda have apologised for enslavement – and a number of countries offer citizenship to diasporans. But these gestures are still either symbolic or individual, and fail to make a dent in the ongoing economic impacts of enslavement. “Addressing this issue is a much more difficult task,” Holsey tells me.
It also requires genuine unity across the diaspora. This shouldn’t revolve around a story of winners and losers, but rather an understanding of the slave trade’s devastating impact on African and Caribbean nations. March’s historic UN resolution, which declared the trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and called for reparations, was tabled by Ghana and coordinated by the African Union – representing this kind of cross-diaspora solidarity.
“The question we should ask is not, ‘What do African nations owe to the African diaspora?’” Holsey says. “Instead, we should ask: ‘How can African nations and the African diaspora work together toward the creation of a more just world?’”
To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.
Tap in
Have you seen division in your own communities around Africa’s role in enslavement? How do you think the diaspora should move forward? Tell us by replying to this or emailing thelongwave@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Insects Don't Swarm at LED Lights
articles.body:
3 November 2026
Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night.
Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED.
Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.)
In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up.
In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night:
Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight.
Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky!
Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED.
In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light: Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED.
We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies.
— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?
Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light.
Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light.
— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?
So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night.
This trait of LEDs is a good thing because UV artificial light at night distracts insects so much that it’s considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis.

articles.title: I’m a “No-Cart Shopper” — How I Spend $61 a Week on Groceries in New York
articles.body:
I’m a “No-Cart Shopper” — How I Spend $61 a Week on Groceries in New York
- Name: Jordan
- Location: Brooklyn, NY
- Number of people in household: Me + 3 roommates
- Age: 37
- Occupation: Baker/bookseller
- Where you shopped: Met Fresh
- Weekly food budget: N/A
- Amount spent: $61.48
Where did you shop?
I live in Bed Stuy, Brooklyn, which has an unfortunately long history of being underserved when it comes to access to quality affordable places to buy groceries. The corner stores and small grocery stores that I have near me don’t have amazing selections of fresh produce or the best prices. I make do throughout the week, but will occasionally trek downtown to stores like Trader Joe’s and Whole Foods where the prices are better and the selection is more consistent.
What’s your grocery strategy?
With my hectic schedule of part-time and freelance work and a long commute, my strategy these days is to get in and out as quickly as possible. Grocery stores in NYC are notoriously crowded during peak hours, and from my experience can be a little overwhelming. I’m a no-cart shopper, preferring to load up my arms or use a shopping basket. 
Being mostly a vegetarian, I shop the produce area first just in case a particular quality vegetable catches my eye. If it does, I’ll use that item as an anchor for the rest of my meal. I’ll then head to the center aisles for canned goods and more pantry heroes. I almost always leave with a can of beans and coconut milk. I can make so many things out of these two ingredients alone. 
How do you meal plan?
This is tough! I wish that I devoted more time to this, but my weeks get so busy that I’m often figuring out dinner during my commute home from work. I get home around 7 p.m. and often have another three to four hours of baking to do, so dinner sometimes looks like popcorn, carrots and hummus, chips and dips, or leftovers if I’ve had enough time to cook earlier in the week. 
When I do have time to plan ahead, I try to focus my meals on groups of three: a protein, a carb, and a vegetable. I usually cook things separately and store them in containers that way so I can remix them throughout the week with different pantry sauces and condiments. 
What did you buy?
Met Fresh
- Baby spinach, $3.99
- Granny Smith apples, $1.34
- Soft tofu, $3.49
- Mango, $1.67
- Kiwi, $0.67
- Seedless English cucumber, $1.50
- Okra, $4.99
- Bread, $7.99
- Celery, $3.99
- Watermelon, $3.61
- Cilantro, $0.69
- Limes, $1.20
- Tomato, $1.49
- Coconut milk, $4.49
- Popcorn, $5.49
- Ginger root, $2.40
- Smoked mussels, $7.99
- Scallions, $2.00
- Onions, $2.49
Grand Total: $61.48
Monday: Oatmeal, Tomato Toast with Smoked Mussels, and Pizza
To start the day, I eat oatmeal with peanut butter, banana, flax seeds, and coconut.
Later, for lunch, I have tomato toast with smoked mussels from Patagonia Provisions. 
For dinner, I don’t cook and instead eat with my friends. We went to a pizza spot by my apartment. 
Tuesday: Muffin, Turkey Sandwich, and Vegetable Curry
During my commute, I get a muffin and coffee for breakfast. 
For lunch, I go to a market by my work and get a turkey sandwich, a slice of carrot cake, roast cauliflower, and a cold brew coffee. 
For dinner, I make a vegetable curry with sweet potatoes, chickpeas, okra, and coconut milk. 
Wednesday: Bagel, Falafel Wrap, and More Vegetable Curry
For breakfast I eat a bagel with peanut butter and sliced bananas. Alongside it is my morning coffee. Today I drink it black. 
For lunch, I eat a falafel wrap that I grab from the bodega on my block with some popcorn and a kombucha. 
I have leftovers from dinner, so I eat more vegetable curry. 
Thursday: Carrot Muffin, Spicy Tofu Sandwich, and Cabbage Jeon with Kimchi
This morning I eat a carrot muffin and an apple, and wash it down with a black cold brew coffee. 
For lunch, I have a spicy tofu sandwich, kettle chips, watermelon, and more cold brew coffee. 
For dinner, I make a cabbage jeon and eat that alongside some kimchi.
Friday: Breakfast Burrito, Tofu Teriyaki, and a Green Smoothie
Today I have a breakfast burrito and a muffin with some more cold brew coffee. I drink cold brew most mornings. 
For lunch, I buy a bowl of tofu teriyaki with vegetables and rice from a place that’s near my work. 
Later in the day, I’m not so hungry so I drink a green smoothie with apple, kiwi, spinach, psyllium husk, celery, and lime juice.
Saturday: Toast, Falafel Wrap, and Green Smoothie
Today starts the weekend. I start my morning with a slice of toast with peanut butter and banana, eat an apple on the side, and drink it with black coffee.
For lunch, I buy a falafel wrap and fries from Lava Shwarma. 
For dinner, I have another green smoothie and some more popcorn.
Sunday: Carrot Bread, Turkey Sandwich, and a Quesadilla
On Sunday I start my day with a slice of carrot bread and have an apple with black coffee. 
For lunch I eat a turkey sandwich with popcorn and a cold brew. 
For dinner I have a black bean, corn, and cheese quesadilla with tortilla chips.

articles.title: Benchfmt.rs: Bringing Go's benchmarking and benchstat workflow to Rust
A New Go API for JSON
articles.body:
The Go Blog
A new Go API for JSON
Introduction
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!
Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.
Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.
After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!
This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json, and an introduction to the new packages.
Problems with encoding/json
Overall, encoding/json has held up well.
The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types
with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to
customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.
However, in the years since its introduction,
various users have identified numerous shortcomings.
Behavior flaws
There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json:
- Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. 
  - encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,
whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.
The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,
instead of introducing silent data corruption,
which may cause problems downstream.
  - encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.
RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,
so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,
merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.
The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value
without a universally agreed upon meaning.
This could be exploited by attackers in security applications
and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635).
The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.
- Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with
programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled
into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.
Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null,
this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.
A survey
indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps
are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.
- Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.
- Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail,
MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver
are inconsistently called by encoding/json. While regarded as a bug,
this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.
API deficiencies
The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:
- It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader.
Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v),
which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.
- Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types,
but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions.
Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces
cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack.
For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect
when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.
- The Compact, Indent, and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer.
This limits the usability of those functions.
Performance limitations
Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:
- MarshalJSON: The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation
to allocate the returned []byte. Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON
and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.
- UnmarshalJSON: The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that
a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data).
This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled
in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON.
Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.
- Lack of streaming: Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate
on an io.Writer or io.Reader, they buffer the entire JSON value in memory.
The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy
and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.
Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method
recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function,
then the performance becomes quadratic.
Trying to fix encoding/json directly
Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.
While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.
We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2,
but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package.
This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2),
where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace
in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1).
Building on encoding/json/jsontext
Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the
encoding/json/jsontext package
that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.
JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:
- syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
- semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.
We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.
This diagram provides an overview of this separation.
Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods.
The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data.
The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package,
contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax,
while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package,
contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data
handled by the bottom half.
The basic API of jsontext is the following:
package jsontext
type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error
type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)
type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind
The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON
at a syntactic level and derives its name from
RFC 8259, section 2
where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text.
Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level,
it does not depend on Go reflection.
The Encoder and
Decoder
provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens.
The constructors
accept variadic options
that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding.
Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1,
the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and
semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.
A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as
a named []byte.
It is identical to RawMessage in v1, which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value.
A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens.
A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type
with constructors and accessor methods.
It is analogous to Token in v1
but is designed represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.
To resolve the fundamental performance problems with
the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods,
we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON
as a streaming sequence of tokens and values.
In v2, we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods
that operate on an Encoder or Decoder, allowing the methods’ implementations
to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not
be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON,
nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value
provided to UnmarshalJSON. These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder.
Introducing encoding/json/v2
Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the
encoding/json/v2 package.
It is designed to fix the problems in v1,
while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package.
Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2.
Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2.
For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to
study the examples in the v2 package,
the “Working with JSON” tutorial, or
read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic.
The basic API of v2 is the following:
package json
func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error
func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error
The Marshal
and Unmarshal functions
have a signature similar to v1, but accept options to configure their behavior.
The MarshalWrite
and UnmarshalRead functions
directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader,
avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder
just to write or read from such types.
The MarshalEncode
and UnmarshalDecode functions
operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and
is actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions.
Unlike v1, options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions,
greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2.
There are several options available
in v2 which are not covered by this article.
Type-specified customization
Similar to v1, v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation
by satisfying particular interfaces.
type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}
type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}
The Marshaler
and Unmarshaler interfaces
are identical to those in v1.
The new MarshalerTo
and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces
allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder.
This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options
can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder.
See the OrderedObject example
for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members.
Caller-specified customization
In v2, the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify
a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type,
where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods
or the default representation for a particular type.
func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options
type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers
func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options
type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers
MarshalFunc and
MarshalToFunc
construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call
using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types.
Similarly,
UnmarshalFunc and
UnmarshalFromFunc
support similar customization for Unmarshal.
The ProtoJSON example
demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all
proto.Message types
to be handled by the protojson package.
Behavior differences
While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1,
its behavior has changed in some ways
to address problems in v1, most notably:
- v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.
- v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.
- v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.
- v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a
case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.
- v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have
encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null, "", [], and {}).
- v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration,
which currently has no default representation,
but provides options to let the caller decide.
For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option
that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics,
or even other caller-determined behavior.
See “Migrating to v2” for more information.
Performance optimizations
The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1.
Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower.
The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1,
with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.
In order to obtain greater performance gains,
existing implementations of
Marshaler and
Unmarshaler should
migrate to also implement
MarshalerTo and
UnmarshalerFrom,
so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner.
For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods
significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes
(see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315),
while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude.
For more benchmark details, see the
go-json-experiment/jsonbench
repository.
On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1.
You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.
Compatibility
The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.
The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise.
Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2.
That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported.
We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together.
Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.
For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package.
That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior.
No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.
Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct.
The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance.
No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood.
We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2.
As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options.
Each behavior difference is controlled by one of the these options.
Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options.
With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo) or new struct tags (e.g., embed) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users.
Migration
Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.
encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2, and which option controls that behaviors.
Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.
For example, we can select all v2 behavior except for allowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(true))
Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except for disallowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(false))
The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2.
More information
For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:
- The “Working with JSON” tutorial,
- The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation,
- The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation,
- and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide.
A long time coming
The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years.
In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package,
Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json) first drafted his
thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like.
Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers,
Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package
needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was
neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the
Protocol Buffer specification required,
nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.
Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable,
Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and
started to build a prototype
(with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module).
Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt)
joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing.
Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our
recorded meetings and
meeting notes.
Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes.
This work has been public since the beginning,
and we increasingly involved the wider Go community,
first with a
GopherCon talk and
discussion posted in late 2023,
formal proposal posted in early 2025,
and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25
for wider-scale testing by all Go users.
The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point,
incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable
empirical experience from use in production settings.
It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.
Thank you to everyone that contributed!

articles.title: A New Go API for JSON
articles.body:
The Go Blog
A new Go API for JSON
Introduction
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!
Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.
Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.
After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!
This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json, and an introduction to the new packages.
Problems with encoding/json
Overall, encoding/json has held up well.
The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types
with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to
customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.
However, in the years since its introduction,
various users have identified numerous shortcomings.
Behavior flaws
There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json:
- Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. 
  - encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,
whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.
The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,
instead of introducing silent data corruption,
which may cause problems downstream.
  - encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.
RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,
so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,
merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.
The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value
without a universally agreed upon meaning.
This could be exploited by attackers in security applications
and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635).
The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.
- Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with
programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled
into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.
Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null,
this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.
A survey
indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps
are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.
- Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.
- Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail,
MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver
are inconsistently called by encoding/json. While regarded as a bug,
this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.
API deficiencies
The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:
- It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader.
Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v),
which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.
- Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types,
but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions.
Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces
cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack.
For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect
when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.
- The Compact, Indent, and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer.
This limits the usability of those functions.
Performance limitations
Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:
- MarshalJSON: The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation
to allocate the returned []byte. Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON
and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.
- UnmarshalJSON: The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that
a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data).
This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled
in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON.
Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.
- Lack of streaming: Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate
on an io.Writer or io.Reader, they buffer the entire JSON value in memory.
The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy
and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.
Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method
recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function,
then the performance becomes quadratic.
Trying to fix encoding/json directly
Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.
While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.
We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2,
but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package.
This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2),
where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace
in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1).
Building on encoding/json/jsontext
Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the
encoding/json/jsontext package
that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.
JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:
- syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
- semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.
We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.
This diagram provides an overview of this separation.
Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods.
The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data.
The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package,
contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax,
while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package,
contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data
handled by the bottom half.
The basic API of jsontext is the following:
package jsontext
type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error
type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)
type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind
The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON
at a syntactic level and derives its name from
RFC 8259, section 2
where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text.
Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level,
it does not depend on Go reflection.
The Encoder and
Decoder
provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens.
The constructors
accept variadic options
that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding.
Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1,
the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and
semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.
A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as
a named []byte.
It is identical to RawMessage in v1, which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value.
A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens.
A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type
with constructors and accessor methods.
It is analogous to Token in v1
but is designed represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.
To resolve the fundamental performance problems with
the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods,
we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON
as a streaming sequence of tokens and values.
In v2, we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods
that operate on an Encoder or Decoder, allowing the methods’ implementations
to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not
be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON,
nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value
provided to UnmarshalJSON. These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder.
Introducing encoding/json/v2
Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the
encoding/json/v2 package.
It is designed to fix the problems in v1,
while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package.
Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2.
Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2.
For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to
study the examples in the v2 package,
the “Working with JSON” tutorial, or
read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic.
The basic API of v2 is the following:
package json
func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error
func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error
The Marshal
and Unmarshal functions
have a signature similar to v1, but accept options to configure their behavior.
The MarshalWrite
and UnmarshalRead functions
directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader,
avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder
just to write or read from such types.
The MarshalEncode
and UnmarshalDecode functions
operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and
is actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions.
Unlike v1, options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions,
greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2.
There are several options available
in v2 which are not covered by this article.
Type-specified customization
Similar to v1, v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation
by satisfying particular interfaces.
type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}
type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}
The Marshaler
and Unmarshaler interfaces
are identical to those in v1.
The new MarshalerTo
and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces
allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder.
This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options
can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder.
See the OrderedObject example
for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members.
Caller-specified customization
In v2, the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify
a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type,
where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods
or the default representation for a particular type.
func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options
type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers
func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options
type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers
MarshalFunc and
MarshalToFunc
construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call
using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types.
Similarly,
UnmarshalFunc and
UnmarshalFromFunc
support similar customization for Unmarshal.
The ProtoJSON example
demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all
proto.Message types
to be handled by the protojson package.
Behavior differences
While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1,
its behavior has changed in some ways
to address problems in v1, most notably:
- v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.
- v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.
- v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.
- v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a
case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.
- v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have
encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null, "", [], and {}).
- v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration,
which currently has no default representation,
but provides options to let the caller decide.
For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option
that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics,
or even other caller-determined behavior.
See “Migrating to v2” for more information.
Performance optimizations
The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1.
Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower.
The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1,
with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.
In order to obtain greater performance gains,
existing implementations of
Marshaler and
Unmarshaler should
migrate to also implement
MarshalerTo and
UnmarshalerFrom,
so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner.
For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods
significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes
(see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315),
while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude.
For more benchmark details, see the
go-json-experiment/jsonbench
repository.
On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1.
You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.
Compatibility
The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.
The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise.
Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2.
That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported.
We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together.
Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.
For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package.
That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior.
No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.
Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct.
The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance.
No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood.
We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2.
As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options.
Each behavior difference is controlled by one of the these options.
Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options.
With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo) or new struct tags (e.g., embed) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users.
Migration
Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.
encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2, and which option controls that behaviors.
Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.
For example, we can select all v2 behavior except for allowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(true))
Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except for disallowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(false))
The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2.
More information
For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:
- The “Working with JSON” tutorial,
- The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation,
- The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation,
- and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide.
A long time coming
The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years.
In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package,
Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json) first drafted his
thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like.
Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers,
Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package
needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was
neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the
Protocol Buffer specification required,
nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.
Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable,
Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and
started to build a prototype
(with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module).
Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt)
joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing.
Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our
recorded meetings and
meeting notes.
Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes.
This work has been public since the beginning,
and we increasingly involved the wider Go community,
first with a
GopherCon talk and
discussion posted in late 2023,
formal proposal posted in early 2025,
and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25
for wider-scale testing by all Go users.
The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point,
incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable
empirical experience from use in production settings.
It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.
Thank you to everyone that contributed!
