articles.title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
articles.body:
This is a guest essay by Jessica Hullman, Ginni Rometty Professor of Computer Science and Policy Fellow at Northwestern University.
In his essay on the role that rigorous proofs play in mathematical advances, Bill Thurston writes that the measure of success in math research is “whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics.” Many recent discussions of AI for science hinge on a tension between understanding and answers. Is science about humans achieving insight, or the archiving of verifiable solutions?
One side prioritizes outputs. Progress is implied to be evident in verifiable proofs of longstanding conjectures and cures for diseases, whether humans were involved in their making or not. The other side argues that human understanding is paramount, because it drives integration of new findings into the canon, because it shapes and inspires the next generation, and so on. But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia.
When Terry Tao posed a thought experiment in a recent talk, asking how comfortable people would be taking a cancer treatment produced by AI, complete with a formal certificate of correctness and a passed phase 3 trial, but without any human understanding how it was found, critics suggested that Tao’s reasoning missed the point. Of course a patient with stage 4 cancer would welcome the treatment.
Other examples concern ambiguity in authorship. Tom Dietterich wrote about arXiv’s growing problem with papers submitted by human authors who seem unlikely to have the expertise to understand the claims. Many questioned in response why accountability – by which I mean being answerable for a claim, able to describe what it rests on and respond when it’s challenged – should matter if verification has been solved. I suggested peer reviewers reserve their expert judgment for texts that don’t get flagged as heavily AI-written, so as to prioritize review as human exchange, but some see this as an obstruction to truth-seeking rather than an attempt to preserve it.
The problem is that if we all agree that outputs matter–that we do care about the solutions to longstanding conjectures, that we do ultimately want to know how to cure diseases–then understanding appears as something separate. It’s cast as a mental state that looks optional next to the cure or the proof itself, and becomes easy to dismiss as a second-order constraint that we tack on because historically we’ve required it to arrive at the solutions in the first place.
When defenders of understanding don’t dispute this separation, they immediately lose the argument. It becomes easy for the side that prioritizes output to peg them as simply not trying hard enough to envision a new future. But the superficial framing of understanding that we keep falling back on obscures deeper concerns that these examples share. They are less about anyone’s mental state than about what happens when something goes wrong. Tao’s scenario turns on the possibility that the AI passed the trial by exploiting a weakness in the trial itself. A paper whose authors can’t explain its claims leaves no one to consult if those claims fail.
Where along the way did we come to believe that scientific value lies in correctness alone?
This intuition is ultimately less about AI than it appears. The inclination to let AI drive science is less a sign of how forward-thinking one is about our future with AI, and more a symptom of a “value-free ideal” that has shaped our thinking since the Cold War era: a view that only epistemic criteria (not ethical and social values) deserve a place in judging what the evidence shows. That it pervades our debates about AI for science is not so surprising; it’s only in the last few decades or so that rejecting the value-free ideal became the philosophical mainstream.
This ideal feeds unrealistic expectations and keeps us from seeing that pushback against the rapid infiltration of AI output into the scientific record is neither anti-AI nor anti-science. The stakes are bigger than any one debate or field. The value-free ideal distorts how we go about seeking truth, causing us to mistake verified results for knowledge. It threatens the human capacities that sustain science, causing us to see criticism and accountability as inconvenient overhead rather than the mechanics of knowledge production. It leaves us confused about what understanding is, and consequently why it matters.
Is science “naturally aligned”?
The social contract for science represents an idealized relationship between science and society that arose after World War II in the US: scientists receive public funding and autonomy, and in return society receives the benefits of their inquiry. Built on a distinction between pure and applied science and a “linear model” in which basic research feeds applied work, the social contract replaces abstract arguments about the value of understanding with practical societal benefits, reshaping how we see science. Drawing on arguments made by concerned scientists in the late 1800s, who worried public celebration of new inventions like electric lights and the steam engine would crowd out respect for what they viewed as their more essential contributions, it also helped to forge a value-free ideal that says that at its core, science must be removed from “contextual values” like ethical or social concerns. For the social contract to gain broad societal buy-in as a model of scientific progress (and consequently shore up government investment in scientific research), we needed to imagine truth-seeking as the impersonal application of methods, immune to political or social pressures.
Philosophers of science aspired to inquiry based only on “epistemic” (or “cognitive”) values. Any influence from the scientist’s intentions or values came to be seen as a risk that the right methods should minimize, laying the groundwork for today’s questions about why it should matter who asserted the claim so long as it’s correct.
Many debates about AI’s role in science come down to disagreements about whether the scientific truth can be realized purely through use of the right procedures. Over the course of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there was almost a moralizing drive to eliminate as much of the scientist’s self as possible from the scientific process, so that trust in individuals could be replaced with trust in the system.
AI agents set loose on the scientific literature, able to verify and intervene experimentally themselves, look like the long-awaited fulfillment of nineteenth century scientific ethics. Much of the “AI for science” rhetoric inherits what I call the “science is naturally aligned” premise: by enacting the scientific method at scale, with its various justification procedures, we can reach a place where we no longer need human judgment to produce truth.

Philosophers of science now predominantly reject the value-free ideal as being appropriate or helpful. Values enter because whether we reject or accept hypotheses is contingent on how we weigh consequences. It was considered solved after peer review exposed an error that led to a corrected version of the original proof, even though formal verification didn’t come until recently. If, as fields are transformed by AI, we stop producing people who can judge what’s interesting and aligned with human aspirations, we may end up with a science that fails to serve basic human interests. As the philosopher Helen Longino argues, the basis for objective public knowledge is a shared language and a belief that things we describe exist independently of how we perceive them. If we can agree on descriptions of the world, then two things become possible: we can defer to others’ experiences to obtain knowledge, and meaningfully criticize scientific claims.
Scientific communities develop shared standards and vocabulary that allow us to build on one another’s findings. We don’t need to verify everything firsthand, and sometimes relying on others’ findings can give us better grounds for believing something than investigating it ourselves, particularly when they possess evidence or expertise that we lack.
Without criticism, we cannot have objectivity; it is, as Longino puts it “dependent upon the depth and scope of the transformative interrogation that occurs in any given scientific community.” For criticism to be transformative requires someone who is obliged to take it up.

Method itself is best understood as a social process, where progress depends on how well a community sustains critical dialogue. This dialogue builds the people in it, shaping what it means for them to understand and exercise judgment along with the knowledge it produces.
If criticism and an ability to trust others’ assertions are integral to the production of knowledge, we might ask whether AI can fulfill these same functions. Can models realize transformative criticism without human involvement? Can we trust the assertions of AI agents without obtaining direct understanding ourselves? And if we do, what happens to our own capacity to question, criticize, and stand behind results?
What does it mean to assert something is true?
The view that it shouldn’t matter who asserted some result as long as it’s correct corresponds to reliabilist epistemologies in philosophy. Classical epistemology insisted that true beliefs are only knowledge if the believer is able to produce reasons for their belief. In contrast, reliabilist epistemologies argue that true beliefs can, at least in some cases, represent genuine knowledge even when the believer can’t produce justifying reasons, provided they arrived at those beliefs by exercising capacities that are reliable producers of true beliefs in those circumstances.
But there are limits to what reliability can provide. The philosopher Robert Brandom imagines a community where the members hold true beliefs, which they have acquired through reliable means, but cannot offer reasons for any of them. Because attributing reliability to the source of their beliefs would itself provide a form of justification based on inference, the community can’t know that they are reliable. They are reliable as instruments indicating something about their surroundings, but unable to recognize themselves as such. Unable to even possess the concept of reliability, Brandom concludes, they cannot have knowledge.
If reliability alone can’t produce knowledge, what can? Brandom’s response is that calling something knowledge is a social act. To call what someone has “knowledge,” we have to attribute to them a commitment (that they believe that thing) along with an entitlement to that belief (that it is justified). But we also have to undertake that commitment ourselves, in the sense that we endorse the belief.
The scientist who first asserted the claim allows us to repeat the claim (and draw conclusions from it) while leaving them responsible for justifying it if challenged. We do this relatively easily in human science because if it turns out there was something wrong with the original assertion, there is an answerable source we can consult to resolve it. Assertions have social significance because we can hold the original author accountable for what was said. This is the sense of understanding that matters most for science, that mathematicians want after the proof has been verified, and that Tao’s patient wants too: results that can be interrogated and reconceptualized where needed, to avoid the perception of progress that fails to serve our goals.
But when we rely on AI results we don’t understand, there is only the person whose name is on the result to turn to. This is the problem arXiv is concerned with: no author can take responsibility for what they cannot understand, and hence they cannot respond to criticism by saying what it rests on, or whether it should be withdrawn. In other words, formal authorship survives while substantive authorship weakens. And so we lose the potential for transformative criticism, which is what sustains our notions of “objective” results in the first place.
Could AI act as an accountable epistemic agent?
A natural question is whether we could put the criticism to the AI agent itself, letting it decide whether to defend the result or concede and revise. What would it mean for AI to be an epistemic agent capable of committing to its assertions?
There are a few challenges with today’s agents that would need to be overcome. One is their lack of persistence and identity in the sense that we attribute it to people. An agent that retracts something it asserted in one session is not bound to maintain its correction or the reasoning behind it in the next. If each new result is produced by a new bespoke multi-agent infrastructure, it becomes hard to “keep score” in the way that naturally happens within networks of human scientists.
Scientific knowledge production depends on epistemic agents who have something at stake. Making bad claims changes the scientist’s standing in the community, which is how trust in individuals can remain calibrated. It’s not clear what comparable loss an AI agent faces in retracting its assertions, particularly given its lack of persistence.
To overcome such limitations would require a considerable shift in how we develop AI: away from being maximally helpful in each exchange and toward being accountable across them, as human scientists tend to be. This may well be possible. But I don’t think accountable AI will be enough to sustain meaningful science from our human perspective.
Let’s say we succeed in developing agents that can answer for claims. This is half of what accountability demands, but we also need others capable of holding them accountable, by asking for evidence, questioning assumptions, recognizing when an answer is evasive. Endorsements of others’ assertions are only as good as our capacity to engage with what we are endorsing.
These are capacities that get built by exercising them, by choosing problems, defending our work, reviewing papers, challenging others’ results. When we don’t exercise our capacities, we lose them. It’s not clear what we gain from a perfectly accountable AI if no one can judge how good its answers are. We’d have truth-seeking in theory, but no one who is able to do it.
Thurston’s notion of mathematical success points to this shared capacity to interrogate, extend, and repair a field’s knowledge that he’s hinting at. As he puts it, “As long as people in the field are comfortable that the idea works, it doesn’t need to have a formal written source.” Verification can tell us a result checks out in a technical sense, but only a community of people prepared to stand behind it can turn it into knowledge.
If we continue to appeal to value-free ideals that frame correctness as all that matters, we will keep building tools that prioritize answers while neglecting the truth-seeking and understanding of the people who can make them count.

But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia.

articles.title: AI stocks slide as Texas governor result raises data center risks
articles.body:
AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.
The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.
He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX were down 4% after the open, and Tesla shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.
Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red.
Tech giants Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%.
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

OpenAI Acquires Pierre Computer to Supercharge Codex
			
		 	
				OpenAI has acquired developer tools startup Pierre Computer Company to strengthen Codex. "The deal, announced today, signals OpenAI's aggressive push into the developer tools market as the AI arms race intensifies," reports The Tech Buzz. Financial terms weren't disclosed. From the report: 
Pierre Computer Company had been building specialized tools for code analysis and review, capabilities that complement Codex's existing strength in code generation. That's a workflow improvement that enterprise engineering teams have been demanding.
[...] For Pierre Computer Company, the acquisition likely provides the resources and distribution that startups in this space desperately need. Building AI developer tools requires massive compute infrastructure and access to cutting-edge models -- both of which OpenAI has in abundance. Pierre's team will now have access to OpenAI's latest models, including the technology behind ChatGPT and the recently announced Shepherd model for AI research validation.
The integration timeline remains unclear, but developers using Codex should expect to see Pierre's capabilities rolling out in the coming months. OpenAI has been moving quickly to ship new features -- it just launched Dots, transforming its coding tools into an always-on AI assistant. Adding Pierre's code review and analysis features could make Codex a genuine end-to-end solution for software development teams.

articles.title: Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
articles.body:
The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG), which oversees the wireless standard, has formally adopted Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) as an optional feature of the Bluetooth Core 7.0. It’s an upgrade the Bluetooth SIG has been previewing over the past year, and it increases Bluetooth LE’s maximum supported bit rate from 2 Mbps to 7.5 Mbps. It will allow for higher-resolution audio streaming as well as improvements to battery life and reliability.
Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
The maximum bit rate of Bluetooth LE will increase by nearly four times.
The primary application for Bluetooth HDT once again will be for wireless audio, with the first devices supporting the new feature expected to appear sometime in 2027. The increased bit rate will support high-resolution audio but also new wireless audio experiences, including spatial audio and multichannel surround sound without requiring proprietary wireless formats.
Bluetooth HDT will benefit other wireless devices beyond headphones. Smartwatches could sync more training, health, and fitness data to a phone without a reduction in battery life because HDT can transfer more data in less time, requiring the Bluetooth radio to be on for shorter periods. Spatial computing and extended reality devices could offer more robust experiences without needing a Wi-Fi connection, and HDT will benefit the ever-growing number of personal AI devices, allowing them to more efficiently hand off data to be processed by a smartphone so they can be lighter and smaller.
Even the simple act of updating the firmware on a smartwatch or smart home accessories could feel faster and become a task that doesn’t need to be put off until later when you’re not using your device. “Bluetooth HDT brings a new level of performance to Bluetooth technology, expanding the role it can play across consumer, commercial, and industrial markets and creating a powerful foundation for the next generation of wireless innovation,” says Neville Meijers, CEO of the Bluetooth SIG. “As the world’s most widely used wireless standard, Bluetooth technology has continually evolved to meet the growing demands of an increasingly connected world.”

articles.title: Democrats win control of the House of Representatives
articles.body:
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans.
The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win about 255 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority.
NBC News has projected the Democrats will also flip control of the Senate, putting them in charge of both chambers.
Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. The blue wave washed over many more GOP-held seats than that — from the East Coast to Texas’ Rio Grande Valley — most in districts that Trump carried in 2024.
A quartet of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Harvie beat GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus; Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti bested GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry, a former chairman of the far-right Freedom Caucus, in the 10th District.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area, while Democrat Shannon Taylor upset longtime GOP Rep. Rob Wittman outside Richmond.
Another big name in Republican politics, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, lost his race for re-election to Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., the first Ukrainian-born member of Congress, who frequently clashed with Trump and GOP leaders, also was defeated. And in Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel trounced GOP Rep. Gabe Evans.
One of the biggest prizes of the night for Democrats was Richard Ojeda II’s upset of Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C. As chairman of the House GOP’s campaign arm, Hudson was responsible for protecting GOP incumbents and the majority.
The Democrats’ victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the prices of gas, groceries and other goods.
When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will be the first time in Trump’s second term that he won’t have full control of Congress.
Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies through the Department of Government Efficiency, unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way.
The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House.
He walked into his election night watch party to raucous cheers as the rap song “Unbelievable,” by the Notorious B.I.G., played on the speakers. The midterm results show the “American people are crying out for transformational change,” Jeffries told supporters.
“Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, in the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea. The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said at the gathering in Washington.
“They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people,” he said, “and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.”
With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump’s administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas.
And in a callback to Trump’s first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that’s the right political path.
Jeffries told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out” on impeachment.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on “Trump family corruption,” including Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize “abuses” by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas: reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump’s war with Iran.
“I wouldn’t characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries told reporters at Democrats’ campaign headquarters before the election.
The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It’s unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him.
House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump’s dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP’s loss.
Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle’s mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage.
Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats.
But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50, which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats.
While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans’ new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
“We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence,” Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress.
“This fight is not over; we’ve just gotten started,” he added. “It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again.”

articles.title: 💧 Toward a More Perfect Union
articles.body:
In what must be seen as a repudiation of Donald Trump’s abhorrent second term as president, as well as the failures of the Republican-controlled House and Senate to actually govern, yesterday’s elections saw voters across America shift left in remarkable numbers. As a result, Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January. When they do, the legislative branch can hopefully return to its proper role providing a check on the executive branch, rather than a rubber stamp for it.
One election isn’t going to solve all the problems in America. Nevertheless, I find myself with a newly restored hope for the future. Even with billionaires (and one odious trillionaire) donating sickening amounts of money in an attempt to buy themselves a government, we can still make progress toward a more perfect union. And if you don’t believe it, consider that yesterday saw the election of America’s first Muslim senator (Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan). It saw the election of our first openly gay senator (Chris Pappas of New Hampshire). We elected our first Black female governor (Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia)1, along with our first female Native American senator and governor (Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Deb Haaland in New Mexico, respectively). That’s a lot of firsts, and you can bet that they won’t be lasts.
Progress toward government that represents all of America is marching on. That’s how it’s supposed to work. It’s nice to see that it still can.
Footnotes:
- I’m not sure which is a funnier name, “Governor Bottoms” or “Governor Lance Bottoms”, but I love it either way. ↩︎

articles.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI
articles.body:
Google was met with swift backlash on Tuesday after it announced that schools using Google’s K-12 software will not be able to use Search unless they opt in to using AI tools.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a student’s school doesn’t opt in to using AI tools like Gemini, then students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
Even as Google made this announcement on a busy Election Day, several left-leaning politicians took time to speak up about their concerns.
Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google in an X post of “extortion,” writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said on X that Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.”
Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair and staunch advocate against monopolies, also condemned Google’s decision as anticompetitive.
“This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” she wrote. “Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.”
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of being a monopoly, commenting, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”
While Search is a necessary tool for information gathering, educators worry that its built-in AI overviews could dissuade students from finding answers themselves. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools, using a different search engine isn’t a simple fix.
Google says that it’s working on a “Guided Learning” tool for student accounts in Search, which is supposed to walk students through the process of solving a problem or finding information, rather than just handing them the answer. If a student is struggling with a math problem, for example, the feature may prompt them to refresh their memory about the rules for dividing exponents, instead of spitting out a number.
In response to the backlash, Google pointed out in a post on X that it had listened to educators by turning off access to AI products by default and noted that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually.
“We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google wrote in its statement. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.”

articles.title: Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson’s Whimsical Books and Dolls Celebrate Black Community
articles.body:
Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson’s Whimsical Books and Dolls Celebrate Black Community
When Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson (1940-2015) was born, her family moved to Columbus, Ohio’s brand new Poindexter Village. The public housing estate, dedicated by Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1940, was one of the first federally funded projects of its kind to specifically support African Americans. (In 2028, a new museum is slated to honor its history.)
Other than a few years’ stint in Boise, Idaho, while she was married to a man serving in the U.S. Air Force, Robinson spent her life in Columbus, where she had also studied art in college. The 1970s spurred a period of growth in the artist’s creative practice, during which she worked for the city’s recreation and parks department and often facilitated workshops. Then, during a study trip to Egypt in 1979, a holy man tendered the name “Aminah,” which she legally adopted and preferred to go by thereafter. In the early 1980s, she exhibited her work for the first time.
In collaboration with the Columbus Museum of Art, where Robinson’s work is a highlight of the collection, Fort Gansevoort presents 25 of the late artist’s works later this month in Beaded and Bound. Spanning a collection of mixed-media books and embellished textiles and dolls, the exhibition features embroidery, appliqué, writing, painting, and drawing in which “the artist wove personal memories, family histories, and local narratives into richly tactile, sometimes peculiar, and always moving works alive with the histories of the African diaspora,” the gallery says.
Robinson’s interest in storytelling is matched by her experimental, almost stream-of-consciousness approach. She described the practice of creating sculptural reliefs on her books as “RagGonNon,” which she considered to be interactive, constantly evolving, and open to interpretation in the way that literature evokes different things for different readers. She viewed her vernacular visual narratives the same way.
The artist also concocted unique combinations of materials, not only assembling different elements such as shells and buttons but also creating distinctive structural substances. Notably, Robinson used a mixture she called “hogmawg,” which consists of clay, leaves, twigs, mud, lime, animal grease, and glue—a process she learned from her father, who had initially taught her the craft of bookmaking. She picked up sewing and needlework from her mother.
Robinson also found a fruitful creative connection with fellow Columbus artist Elijah Pierce, whom she described as a spiritual mentor and friend. “He was a great person, a great artist, and a person who walked with integrity, and he passed on so much of that wisdom to me,” she once said. “We just generally like to be around each other. There was just a connection there.”
Through textural, whimsical narratives, Robinson’s books and dolls are simultaneously autobiographical and universal. “A Holy Place: The Elijah Pierce Barbershop,” for example, depicts her friend in his place of work, nodding to a meaningful personal relationship but also celebrating more broadly the barbershop as a “sacred” place of connection and joy in African American communities. “Women in Poindexter Village, Button Beaded Book” references fellow residents on the estate, including a special tribute to her mother tucked inside.
Beaded and Bound opens on November 19 and continues through January 16 in New York City.

articles.title: Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
articles.body:
Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent.
Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
Google says AI is boosting searches, but that activity isn’t translating into faster growth for the business that pays for it.
That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions.
“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades.”
Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.”
It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search.
YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026
“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge. AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business.
What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. They’re looking to buy shoes rather than get an AI explanation of them.
Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time.
Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app, saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when.
The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools.
For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets.
“If people are clicking through less often. That is a challenge that they need to figure out.”
“We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says.
The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. Taylor suspects it’s mostly the former.
That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces.
“If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.”
The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. But platforms still have to identify which parts of a conversation matter and match them with the right ads.
“It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says.
An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform.
Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for. Someone searching Google for Nike shoes may already be ready to buy, while someone asking an AI tool which running shoes to choose is still researching. A higher sales return could reflect that difference in purchase intent rather than more effective ads.
Google’s existing business has given it room to take its time with AI ads, Taylor says. He points to its successful shift to mobile: Early phone traffic was less valuable to advertisers because shopping on a phone was cumbersome, but that changed.
Elliott cautions that finding effective ad formats can take years. Search engines started with banner ads before adopting paid listings; social media went through its own experimentation. Today’s formats may not be the ones that ultimately work.
But Google’s mounting AI spending raises the stakes. Search revenue is still growing by double digits, but the company has yet to show how well its new way of searching can pay.
“They absolutely do not have it all figured out,” Elliott says. “No one has it all figured out.”

articles.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
articles.body:
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.
Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title: SpaceX is working with Qualcomm to build its Starlink Mobile 5G network
articles.body:
SpaceX is teaming up with Qualcomm to build out its nationwide mobile network. Under the multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing technology to “tens of thousands” of 5G cell sites across the US, with the first deployments set for 2027.
SpaceX is working with Qualcomm to build its Starlink Mobile 5G network
Qualcomm’s ‘biggest 5G deal yet’ is with SpaceX.
Qualcomm’s ‘biggest 5G deal yet’ is with SpaceX.
The news of the partnership comes as part of SpaceX’s push to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US, competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The Elon Musk-owned company has already snapped up a swath of spectrum, while recent reports suggested that SpaceX was exploring an acquisition of Boost Mobile.
Now, SpaceX is planning to use Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure, a platform made up of hardware and software designed to boost network coverage, capacity, and efficiency. SpaceX plans to combine this infrastructure with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.
“Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today,” Durga Malladi, Qualcomm’s executive vice president and general manager of technology planning, edge solutions, and data center, says. He adds that the companies have the opportunity to “lay the foundation” for 6G in the coming years.

articles.title: French Blood Banks Hit Alongside Cyberattack On European Supermarkets
articles.body:
French Blood Banks Hit Alongside Cyberattack On European Supermarkets (yahoo.com) 29
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: The refrigerators at three regional blood banks in France were hit by a cyberattack overnight between Sunday and Monday, at the same time hackers struck supermarkets from Sweden to Belgium. "Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems," the health ministry said in a statement.
The incident had no impact on blood supplies, EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois said. "We have staff round the clock since blood can be needed at any time. They were warned about the problems by alerts and moved the blood to other refrigerators that were not connected," she said. [...] Investigations are under way into how the attack was carried out, what equipment may have been affected and when systems can safely return to service. The attack followed a similar incident in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phones are up to 27 percent off
articles.body:
You can save a heck of lot of money on Google’s Pixel 11 phones through November 8th, whether you want the best-for-the-least Pixel 11, or the slightly pricier Pixel 11 Pro that takes better photos. Even the big Pixel 11 Pro XL with a longer-lasting battery is hundreds off its original price.
Google’s Pixel 11 phones are up to 27 percent off
With prices up to $350 off, it’s a good time to consider upgrading if you’re looking for a great Android phone.
The Pixel 11 Pro deal is the most attractive of the bunch, as the $1,099.99 phone with 256GB storage and 12GB of RAM is down to just $799.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and at the Google Store, beating its October Prime Day price by $50. It’s $100 less than the base Pixel 11 model sold for at launch, and it’s the phone to get if you want great camera performance, plus extra features like HiLight that, while cool, weren’t really worth paying a premium to access. I’d be very surprised if the price dropped more for Black Friday.
There’s absolutely nothing wrong with opting for the Pixel 11 instead, especially at its attractive $699.99 ($200 off) price that now matches the cost of the iPhone 17E, following Apple’s September price bump. The Pixel 11 is the most affordable phone that supports Google’s software features that are exclusive to this year’s phones, including Magic Capture, Camera Looks, and Proactive Assistance. It has fast 25W wireless charging (up from 15W with the Pixel 10), and has 12GB of RAM, like the Pixel 11 Pro.
I’m still happily rocking my Pixel 9 Pro, but if I were going to upgrade right now, I’d get the Pixel 11 Pro. Yes, I want the better cameras and HiLight. But really, the main reason I’m lured to the Pro is because the trade-in offers are really generous right now. It’s just $10 more to opt for the Pro over the base Pixel 11. My base Pixel 9 Pro with 128GB of storage can fetch $530 in trade-in credit at the Google Store and $525 at Best Buy, which seems great.

articles.title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
articles.body:
Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works
A hands-on look at dual-booting Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, the GPU clock throttling bug found, and why WSL still wins.
Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop?
Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read.
TL;DR
- Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly.
- A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown.
- GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it.
- Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly: Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9.
- Memory allocation is a separate headache, since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM.
- WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today, since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM.
- A real fix depends on Nvidia, specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark.
Remy.
What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC?
The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM.
That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place.
Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance.
How do you actually install Linux on it?
The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot.
Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel.
Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration.
Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps.
How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL?
This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower.
Nothing gets lost.
The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed.
Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power.
Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down?
The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line.
Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back.
The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver.
Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now?
For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs.
The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly.
Frequently Asked Questions
Can the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop dual-boot Windows and Linux?
Yes. Dual-booting was demonstrated on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop using Omarchy, a Linux distribution that already included Nvidia’s open kernel driver for this chip, after an initial attempt with Debian required manual driver and networking workarounds.
Why is Linux so much slower than Windows on this laptop when plugged in?

- app.use(cors())
✓ Tests passed · ready for PR
A Windows-only firmware component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power sharing between the CPU and GPU. Without a Linux equivalent, the GPU’s clock speed gets locked around 780 MHz when the laptop is connected to power, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows.
Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem?
It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect.
Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark?
Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM.

articles.title: Le Creuset’s Best-Selling Dutch Ovens Are on Early Sale for Black Friday (and Selling Out Fast)
articles.body:
Le Creuset’s Best-Selling Dutch Ovens Are on Early Sale for Black Friday (and Selling Out Fast)
This is the time of year when I really lean into cozy cooking. So naturally, it’s also the time when I really lean on my Dutch oven — a piece of cookware durable enough to withstand hours on the stove or in the oven. It’s truly a star player in my kitchen during the fall and winter months (although I do use it all year round, especially for baking sourdough). 
If you don’t have one yet, or you’re looking to upgrade, I’ve got great news: Le Creuset is offering steep discounts on three popular Dutch ovens. Each one is over $100 off right now. So if you’ve been waiting for the right time to snag a beautiful Le Creuset Dutch oven, this is it.
1. Traditional Oval Dutch Oven
Available in six stunning shades, Le Creuset’s Traditional Oval Dutch Oven usually goes for $415 but is on sale right now for $260. Its oval shape makes it perfect for roasts, like chicken, turkey, prime rib, and pork tenderloin. It would also be amazing for big, family-sized pasta bakes. The enameled cast iron Dutch oven works on all stovetops (induction included) and is also oven-safe up to 500°F. It’s dishwasher-safe, too.
2. Signature Round Wide Oven
The enameled cast iron Signature Round Wide Oven has a 6.75-quart capacity, which makes it great for making big, cozy meals. It’s available in 22 colors, including the new teal Riviera, forest green Foret, smoky gray Chateau, and glossy black Onyx. (The recently re-released lavender color, Provence, already sold out.) It’s also dishwasher-safe, oven-safe to 500°F, and compatible with all stovetops. Now you just have to decide which color you want …

I’ve been a journalist for nearly a decade and have tested hundreds of products for the kitchen, home, and beyond since 2022. Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. Democrats were favoured in enough House seats to take the chamber without winning any of the 18 seats the Cook Political Report classed as “toss-ups”. If they won every seat they were expected to win, they would comfortably win a majority. The balance of power rested on whether Democrats would hold the 18 seats rated “lean Democratic”.
