Senate results
Thirty-three of the 100 members of the upper chamber were being elected regularly this year, along with two other special elections. Republicans had the Senate majority before the election. Senators serve six-year terms.
Election explained
House results
Republicans were defending a majority in the 435-member House. Democrats held 212 House seats and needed 218 to win control. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms and face re-election every even year.
Election explained
Governor results
Gubernatorial elections were taking place in 36 states, as well as three territories. Republicans and Democrats held 18 of these state governorships each before the election. Three incumbent governors were retiring.
Election explained
Election explained
How the elections work
The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?
The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.
The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.
How is the Senate elected and how do they work?
The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.
Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.
In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.
Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.
In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.
Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.
How are governors elected and how do they work?
Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.
In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.
Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.
How are the results reported?
The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.
Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.
Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

articles.title: Bethesda Confirms The Elder Scrolls 6 Is Called 'Sentinel'
articles.body:
Bethesda Confirms The Elder Scrolls 6 Is Called 'Sentinel' 19
			
		 	
				During a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, the studio officially confirmed that The Elder Scrolls VI will be titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. "Thank you for 40 years of shared memories," wrote Bethesda in a separate tweet. "We can't wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it'll be some time before we're ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you." Video Games Chronicle reports:  "You know, as we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Bethesda's executive producer Todd Howard said in the video, walking past a display case. "And you know, every day when I walk by this case, obviously I look at the games and think about them, but more so I think about the teams that made them, and the time and the passion that everybody put into the games. And then what they meant to all of you, and hearing from you, and the time that you spent in them, how meaningful that was to you, and to let you know when we hear that, how meaningful that is to us.
And so even though yes, we're looking back, we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called." The video then showed the logo for the game.

articles.title: Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream
articles.body:
Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream (zdnet.com) 48
			
		 	
				Mozilla is testing a new Firefox Nightly feature called Mini Window that lets users pop an entire webpage into a small, always-on-top window stripped of most browser controls. "The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window," writes ZDNet's Jack Wallen. "Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app." From the report:  At first blush, there's no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it. However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/forward/reload buttons, and the window close button -- and that's it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.
On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I'm working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy. [...] Let's say I'm writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them -- even when working on a smaller display.
Here's another use case I've found: When using MacOS's Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window. Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

articles.title: Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter
articles.body:
AI agents won’t be stealing Uber’s lunch any time soon.
Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter
Despite growing concerns over AI disintermediation, Uber executives revealed that third-party bots accounted for just four rides and 500 food deliveries out of 320 million transactions.
Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning. The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording “around 500” during the week of Halloween, out of a total 320 million Uber rides and Uber Eats deliveries.
This is the first time that Uber has disclosed the number of third-party AI agents that have arranged deliveries or rides on its platform. With the rise of AI agents like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, some experts are predicting that platforms like Uber and DoorDash are at risk of disintermediation, in which customers use AI agents to order food or book a ride, rather than visiting the app itself.
But in these early days, it seems like the risk is still very small. During the call, Uber’s executives expressed an openness to working with third-party AI companies to make things easier for agents to use their platform — while also expressing confidence that their customers will continue to prefer the experience of using the Uber app directly.
“We hope that there will be more traction,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the call. “We do think that we want to make services that are available to consumers in a delightful, easy way. We think our direct services are going to be the most delightful and easy, but we will work with these third parties.”
He continued, “It is just very, very early, and we want to make sure we are not dependent on any one player, and I think we are very well positioned in this environment going forward.”
As we’ve noted before, this first wave of AI agents still have a long way to go before people begin seeing them as a viable way to order food or book a ride somewhere. There still is a lot of friction points. And platform operators like Uber or DoorDash have little incentive to allow these agents to barge in and replace their own customers.
Which is not to say the AI companies won’t inevitably figure it out! These companies know this is one of their primary use cases, and their best path to a more profitable future. But getting Uber to agree to more disintermediation will be a tough ask.
Uber is developing its own AI tools that are designed to keep customers using its own platform. Earlier this year, the company rolled out a new Cart Assistant for Uber Eats, in which an AI bot will build a grocery list based on an image of a recipe or a text prompt.

articles.title: All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake
articles.body:
Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is scheduled to release on November 5th. You can follow along with all of our coverage of the game right here.
- The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time never gets old Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom. As a result, Zelda has never been bigger, and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past. Or so it seemed. For one of the biggest Switch 2 exclusives so far, Nintendo has gone back to Ocarina of Time, which originally launched on the N64 in 1998. It’s one of the most influential and revered games in the long-running franchise, a game that showed that the classic Zelda formula — one that used a large world to connect a handful of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons, creating a grand adventure — could work in three dimensions. Now Ocarina has been remade for the Switch 2 in a way that accomplishes exactly what a good remake is designed to do: preserve the core of the original experience while making it more accessible for modern audiences. And it shows there’s still some life left in the traditional Zelda formula. Read Article >
- Keep on rolling. For the Ocarina of Time remake, Nintendo developers said in a new interview that they wanted to “preserve the experience of spamming the Roll Attack to forward roll your way across Hyrule Field.” I have very fond memories of rolling around the world in the original. In the remake, you can still spam Roll Attack, but you can also dash.
- A link to the past. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches later this week, and in the lead-up Nintendo has put out the first half of a lengthy developer Q&A, covering everything from what changed gameplay-wise, to the new visual style, which was inspired by puppet shows. As art director Aya Shida explains: Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds. We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game.
- New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November. Read Article >
- There’s one week left to preorder the Ocarina of Time remake for $10 off The long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 launches next Thursday, November 5th. In other words, you have a week remaining to secure your physical edition with a $10 discount at Amazon and Walmart. Once the game launches, the physical version will almost certainly go from $59.99 to $69.99 while the digital version will stay at $59.99. Nintendo had the unenviable task of reimagining its Nintendo 64-era masterpiece for the Switch 2, and based on our hands-on time with some sections of the game, it’s a lot of fun to play. The graphics and art style are fantastic, and the controls have been modernized to be simpler to pick up for those who are already experienced with third-person action games, including other modern Zelda titles. Read Article >
- Here’s Nintendo’s overview trailer for the Ocarina of Time remake. I’ve really warmed up to the game’s art style, especially in this new trailer. And after reading my colleague Cameron Faulkner’s hands-on preview, I’m looking forward to returning to Hyrule even more. The game launches on Switch 2 on November 5th.
- The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original. More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button. Read Article >
- Hori’s electronic Ocarina of Time requires no musical talent. It was briefly shown during Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct today, but Hori’s website now has a listing for its $49.99 electronic ocarina. You can play your own songs by pushing buttons, play one of 12 pre-programmed songs from the games, use it with the Ocarina of Time remake’s sound recognition feature, or connect headphones for a private jam session.
- Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake launches in November Link’s next adventure now has a release date. During a Legend of Zelda stream for the franchise’s 40th anniversary, Nintendo announced that the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 is launching on November 5th. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI. Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.” Read Article >
- Nintendo is playing things too safe Tuesday’s Nintendo Direct showcase felt like an important moment for the company. With the Switch 2 heading into its second holiday season, one in which the hardware will be even more expensive thanks to a price hike, it was a chance for Nintendo to really sell new audiences on its latest console — but that’s not exactly what happened. While there were some impressive-looking titles, there wasn’t much that felt truly new. Instead, the two major Switch 2 exclusives that will round out the 2026 calendar are both remakes from the Nintendo 64 era. If you missed it, the final reveal of the Direct was a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2. We don’t know when, exactly, it’s launching, but Nintendo says it’ll be out this year. The brief teaser didn’t reveal much of what the game will look like, nor how it might differ from the N64 original, so chances are you can expect an Ocarina-focused Direct in the coming months that will detail more. Whenever it comes out, the Ocarina remake will follow the Star Fox remake, which is launching later this month in an attempt to revitalize Nintendo’s long-dormant sci-fi series for modern audiences. Read Article >
- The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is getting a remake for the Switch 2 Nintendo announced a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time during its Nintendo Direct presentation on Tuesday. It will launch sometime in 2026 on Nintendo Switch 2. More details will be announced “in the future.” This new title is the first major release in the franchise since 2024’s Echoes of Wisdom, which starred Princess Zelda herself. Echoes followed 2023’s Tears of the Kingdom, a direct sequel to Breath of the Wild — both of which got upgraded Switch 2 versions alongside the launch of the new console last year. In November, Nintendo also launched the hack-and-slash title Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment. Read Article >

articles.title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
articles.body:
An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together
By danielrh
When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.
In the beginning we were searching for where we were
On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.
The actual quote
“I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source
This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.
Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.
(snapshotorigin ⊙ snapshotlater) ∧ (snapshotorigin ⊕ snapshotmoved)
There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be.  I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2. I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.
CAE2, since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped. 
I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.
Then we searched for what we faced
I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.
To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F. However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D. Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff. Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps.  Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.
I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.
It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.
Then we searched for how to act
December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.
Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187  and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.
We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above.
00			terminates any string pointing here.
pushf; pusha		the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them
xor si,si; push si	argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument
call far 12D7:0156	through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded
pop si; popa; popf	cdecl: caller cleans the arguments
retf			back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed
We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate.
In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop (0560:20E3) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player.
Then we tried to bring together fields from afar
In August of 2017, we authored the networking protocol which was a simple TCP client/server architecture with protobuf game messages. Every frame every ship's position would be sent from the leader plus fire events, despawning and damages. The client would reply with its own position, if any lasers were fired or if some cataclysmic event had happened (ejection, landed, died).
Each player would have their own craft as entity 0 and the other player as entity 1, which required a swap when receiving packets from the other emulator.
These packets modified memory directly or were added to a job queue of events that had to happen that frame.
We started with a very simple trampoline:
pushf
pusha
nop
popa
popf
retf
When Borland's overlay loader swaps a code page in, it walks the chain of saved BP frames on the stack and patches any return address that points into an overlay. The hand-made stub had no frame, so the walk read garbage and the game died at random moments. This was a constant thorn in our side from October to December.
The fix was to make the trampoline look like a Borland function:
push bp
mov bp, sp
nop (0x90) ; welcome to the 0x90's
pop bp
retf
We configured DOSBox to notice when the program counter reached the nop and instead inject its call from the job queue of things that should happen. The job queue was based on what was necessary to make the game function correctly in a multiplayer scenario.
In October 2017 we noticed that ephemeral objects would be located in different slots for different players. Having the new hook from DOSBox also let us determine when the function had returned, so we could note down which numeric slot a new ship or projectile had been spawned into.
Ephemeral objects had their own spawn rules and could occupy shared areas of the 61 entity slots. We modified the location that ephemeral objects were placed in so we could confine them to slots 12 to 15 and keep multiplayer locations consistent.
In December we decided to change the client to store a mapping of server ship IDs to local IDs, so we could stop forcing the spawn function return. This allowed packets to translate between local and host IDs. Finally asteroids started to work in multiplayer.
In 2018 we focused on animating explosions, missiles, and autopilot.
The search continued for both success and defeat
In June of 2019 we noted the mission victory calculation was flaky and finicky. We decided to conduct a binary search to find the location of the actual victory point tally. We copied the entire 64K data segment across the network, and slowly cut it in half. After many bisections, we located 80 bytes at 13D3:D248 which held the mission tree. And in October we found the overall victory point counter at 13D3:C280 and mission numbers at 13D3:C255 and C256, which allowed us to select the mission to play from a dropdown, years later.
And finally the joy of combined words
In early 2020, we identified the function that played comm text. This allowed us to send chat over the network and hook typed chat directly into the system so it played using the wingman's VDU. It allowed a very immersive way to chat that reminded us of some of the frenetic sequences in the game.
Some final work in 2020 left the game in a playable state, but we were out of ideas on how to actually share the fun with friends. Expecting people to locate a copy of that old game, compile or download a strange version of DOSBox, share each other's public IPs and punch the firewalls and play together was sadly a bridge too far.
We had a few family playthroughs but the game rested on GitHub, mostly idle.
And in 2026, machine assisted development helped us laugh together
Until now. With the advent of widespread WebRTC, robust emscripten support, and a new system we put together called lobbylink, the time seemed right to revive the project and share it more widely.
lobbylink
I built https://github.com/danielrh/lobbylink which is a simple golang lobby system, depending only on a websocket library, that orchestrates peer to peer WebRTC connections. It can run on any small server and simply allows players to connect to one another using WebRTC and a shared room code. The server has a static allowlist of origins and can let browsers or client software in almost any language connect to it with a room code. The room code is used to locate other players with the same room code and they get notified of all joiners in that room. The server also runs coturn and mints TURN credentials in its joined reply, so players behind restrictive firewalls can join.
I ported over the transport to lobbylink and asked an LLM to configure the build scripts to target emscripten and take a GOG Inno Setup installer package of Wing Commander and unzip it and use it as data files for emscripten. The combination of these makes it possible to download Wing Commander from GOG, drag and drop it into the client-side browser storage, enter a room code, and play.
The game is playable at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox/ and the emulator is at https://github.com/danielrh/wcmulti.
And as an added bonus I asked an LLM to add voice chat as well for realtime voice in game using a second WebRTC peer connection to carry audio, if people choose. And so we can fly and laugh together.

articles.title: Education Shouldn't Be Held for Ransom
articles.body:
An open letter to the tech industry
If you ask any educator what the key to learning is, they won't say it's finding the right answer. They'll say it's what you gain from the struggle of getting there. Learning is found in the time and effort spent trying to understand an idea before it just "clicks."
That's what makes Google's latest announcement so galling to educators. Google announced this week that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for K-12 Google Workspace for Education accounts.
On the surface it sounds like a win for schools until you read the fine print: Google Search will be switched off along with them. Google's explanation, from Chris Phillips, its vice president for education, speaking to The New York Times, is that "Search and AI are deeply integrated," so one cannot be switched off without the other.
After the backlash, Google walked part of it back, saying schools could switch on Search by itself, without the rest of its Gemini products. But the core problem remains. Search still can't be used without AI features like AI Overviews.
The educators asking for choice aren't anti-technology. They have spent years in the classroom, and they know firsthand that handing kids AI-generated answers doesn't build critical thinking; it weakens it.
Search is how students reach the open web. A search engine that arrives only with AI attached isn't offering a choice. It's holding education for ransom.
Learning to search is learning to think
A search engine is really an engine of discovery. When we search, we reflect, weigh, question, and synthesize, all at once. We’re exposed to rival sources and clashing perspectives, and we need sharp critical-thinking skills to discern the quality and relevance of what we find.
Technology companies are optimizing for speed. They talk about "removing friction," which is fine for unimportant things. There’s no benefit to friction when ordering takeout or getting a ride to the airport. But the same doesn't hold for education, because effort is the education. Friction, struggle, and perseverance is the learning. You simply can't speed-run understanding.
It helps to compare classroom learning with other kinds of training.
Imagine runners on the track team riding golf carts around the oval during "training" because the carts are faster and easier than running. They wouldn’t be preparing themselves to succeed in competition. That’s not how athletic training works. Progress is built out of sweat and discomfort.
Imagine band practice consisting of nothing but listening to Spotify, with no one painstakingly struggling to master their instruments or sheet music.
Science, math, and history are no different from athletics and music.
The best teachers rarely answer questions directly. They answer a question with a question of their own. The point isn't to hand over the answer but to make students wrestle with the question until they work it out on their own.
Likewise, a librarian doesn't hand you answers. A librarian's goal is to help you sharpen your research question and steer you toward better sources. That's the kind of help students need right now, especially in a world where the internet is being flooded by low quality AI slop. What students need more than ever are tools that teach them how to think, not what to think.
Information literacy is a practice, not a lesson
The educators I talk to aren't asking for a “magic wand.” They're asking for common-sense safeguards and controls that protect students at every grade level. This is scaffolding to make learning appropriate for all learners.
There’s nothing inherently wrong with giving students an AI answer occasionally, depending on the situation. But over-reliance can quickly turn into outsourcing the very thinking they’re in school to learn. The result over time is the acceptance without challenge of any information presented by AI. This is especially problematic when AI "hallucinates" or fabricates information.
Educators should get to decide when and how AI shows up for their students. Not a vendor. And certainly not under threat of losing basic access to web search.
Follow the incentives
Google is a successful company because they do a great job serving their customers. Unfortunately for educators and students, Google’s customers are advertisers, not users.
Google is the world's largest advertising company, so it's important to understand that when a search engine is funded by ads, it makes every user the product. Google's own founders saw this coming. In a 1998 Stanford paper they warned that advertising-funded search engines "will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."
So when Google tells schools that Search and AI can't be separated, we need to ask who this serves. Is it because it isn’t technically feasible or simply because it isn’t in the best interest of Google advertisers and shareholders?
When educators ask for choice or a slowdown of AI in education, it isn’t because it benefits them directly. It’s because their incentives are aligned with student incentives and they believe in slower, evidence-based approaches over experimenting on kids with brand-new technologies.
At Kagi, we believe in choice
Like Google, Kagi also does a great job serving our customers. The difference is that Kagi’s customers are the users. We build tools that are in the best interest of the people using them. That's why we created Kagi Search with a different user-aligned model. Instead of building at the expense of users, we seek to empower our users with choice.
Our users pay us in order to NOT be the product. And in return we give them the best search with no ads, no tracking and no selling of data. Because when the user is the customer, the user's interests and the company's interests are aligned and in harmony.
For schools, this means:
- AI is optional, not required. Quick Answer only appears when a student asks for it, and schools can turn AI features on or off for the students who are ready.
- Schools stay in control. Block low-quality or distracting sites for everyone, raise trusted sources, and build custom Lenses with teacher-approved resources for class projects
- Fewer dead ends. Students can see when a result is paywalled before they click, instead of hitting a wall mid-research.
- Less noise. Kagi has no ads and no clickbait thumbnails. But it does have filters that hide AI-generated slop images, so students can focus on the information itself.
- Tools that guide, not answer. We're building features that empower students to refine their research questions and search better.
Our ask
To Google and the rest of the industry: Let’s stop putting corporate profits over the civilizational imperative to truly educate students. Let’s give schools choice over coercion and lock-in.
To schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and Kagi is one of them.
Kagi for Education
Your students shouldn't have to accept AI to use search. Kagi gives schools clean, ad-free results with AI off by default, and the controls to decide when it comes on.
Contact us for a quote or a free trial for your school or district.
By Kevin Elgan
Kevin Elgan is Head of Marketing at Kagi and has spent over 15 years in education technology working alongside educators. In prior roles he trained thousands of teachers to use technology effectively in the classroom.

articles.title: This Month in Ladybird – October 2026
articles.body:
Hello friends! In October, we moved style and layout off the main thread, built a JavaScript JIT, replaced our WebAssembly engine, redesigned the browser UI, and passed Safari Technology Preview on Web Platform Tests. :^)
Sponsors
Ladybird is entirely funded by companies and individuals who believe in the open web. You can see everyone supporting the project on our sponsors page, and we’re grateful to all of them. If you’re interested in sponsoring, please contact us.
Style and layout no longer wait for JavaScript
Browsers normally run JavaScript, style, and layout on one main thread, one at a time. While a script runs, the page can’t update. A few simple animations can keep going on the compositor, but everything else has to wait.
We moved style and layout to their own thread, and paint recording to another (#12377, #12400). They now run at the same time as JavaScript (#12396, #12432, #12460). If a script asks for layout information, like an element’s size, it waits until pending layout work is finished, so it never gets stale data.
So two things now work during a long script:
-   CSS animations keep running while JavaScript is busy.  This includes animations that change layout, like width and font-size (#12433, #12447, #12451).
- :hover keeps working while JavaScript is busy.  The render thread finds the element under the mouse, applies its hover styles, starts any transitions, updates the cursor, and draws a new frame. When the script ends, the main thread catches up and fires the hover events (#12530).
As far as we know, no other browser can do this today. Here’s a text animation while JavaScript blocks the main thread in 1.5 second bursts, with Ladybird in the top left:
And here’s :hover on a page running JavaScript for 250ms at a time, with Ladybird on the left and Chrome on the right:
You can also try it yourself. The button blocks the main thread for three seconds. Most browsers keep the square spinning, but freeze the bar and the hover target.
transform width :hover A JavaScript JIT
On Linux and macOS, LibJS now compiles hot JavaScript to machine code, on both x86-64 and AArch64 (#12613).
We decided against a JIT in the past, and did what we could to push and tune the interpreter instead. It’s already competitive, so making it twice as fast would be a huge effort, and that would only turn a 300ms hang into a 150ms hang, which you’d still notice. So we needed an optimizing JIT.
The design is deliberately boring: speculative optimization based on runtime type profiling, like other JavaScript engines. For now, we just want to go reasonably fast.
While code warms up, we record things like which types and object shapes it sees (#12588). The compiled code uses those recordings to make guesses, like “this value is always an integer”, and inlines small functions (#12595, #12598).
To find bugs during development, we used a fuzzer that ran the same code in the JIT and the interpreter and compared the results (#12601).
A new WebAssembly engine
We replaced our C++ Wasm engine and Cranelift with a new engine that has its own interpreter and JIT (#12963). It supports newer parts of WebAssembly that the old engine didn’t, like exception handling and GC. On the JetStream 3 Wasm workloads both engines can run, it scores about 7x higher.
In July, we built flap, a small language and compiler for writing LibJS’s interpreter. The Wasm interpreter is written in flap too, so one source builds it for x86-64, AArch64, and Windows x64. Hot functions move from there to the JIT, even in the middle of a running loop.
We’re making great progress on performance. JSLinux, an x86 PC emulator, now boots Alpine Linux to a shell in 1.8 seconds, while Chrome takes 1.5.
Benchmarks
Web Platform Tests (WPT)
On October 26, we passed Safari Technology Preview on WPT. :^) We ended the month at 2,184,722 subtests, a gain of 75,650.
Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.
A new browser UI
Until now, our UI had grown organically, with tinkering here and there. This was the first time we sat down and mapped out a complete design. We kept it modest and quiet, so the attention stays on the page.
It covers tabs, toolbars, menus, and our own about: pages on macOS and Linux, in light, dark, and a violet dark theme for private windows (#13271, #13169, #12815).
- Tabs: you can pin tabs, search all open tabs, and restore your windows on launch (#12757, #13271).
- Form controls got a new look, and date and time inputs got a picker (#13554).
- Scrolling: smooth mouse wheel scrolling (#12593), elastic overscroll on macOS (#12624), touchpad momentum on other platforms (#12345), and scrollbars that hide until used (#12997).
Sites that work better
- Google Slides: presentations open instead of showing an error (#12497).
- GitHub: Mermaid diagrams render (#12383).
- ChatGPT: the text box grows as you type (#13050).
- nytimes.com and reuters.com get past their bot checks (#12718, #12188).
- Instagram: videos show their first frame instead of staying blank (#12898).
- Gmail: reloading no longer keeps the old page in memory (#12689, #12660).
- x86CSS , an x86 emulator made of CSS, is now usable (#12911).
New browser features
- Screen readers: we’ve added first support for VoiceOver on macOS and Orca on Linux (#9156). There’s still a lot of work to do here.
- Spell checking in text fields on macOS (#12638).
- Picture-in-Picture (#12542).
- Links to text: links can scroll to a piece of text and highlight it, and you can create them from the context menu (#11121, #12744).
- Permissions: sites can now ask for your location and microphone (#13336, #12604).
- DevTools: Inspect Element (#13348), console autocomplete (#13355), and expandable objects in the console (#13360).
- Smaller additions: Find in page can highlight all matches (#12434), ad blocking can be turned off per site from the toolbar (#12695), and we added Reload Without Cache (#13056).
More of the web platform
We rendered this page in Ladybird, using features that landed in October:
From the top left, that’s multi-column (#13026), display: grid-lanes for masonry (#13236), MathML (#13062, #13141), corner-shape (#12942), CSS Motion Path (#13027), much more of anchor positioning (#13021, #13079, #13166), and text-wrap: balance (#13461).
We also added:
-   CSS:  calc-size(), which lets heights animate to and from auto (#13006), plus vertical writing modes (#13103), zoom (#13237), the stretch sizing keyword (#13006), shape() and border-shape (#12942), field-sizing (#13050), view progress timelines and animation-range (#12943), and the start of SVG animation (#12823, #13498).
-   Web APIs and more:  the HTML Sanitizer API (#13185), Touch Events (#13249), Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (#12296), Paint Timing, Event Timing, Largest Contentful Paint (#13110), WebVTT cues (#12895), wide-gamut canvases (#13097), WebDriver BiDi (#13167), JavaScript’s using and await using (#13102), and many execCommand and contenteditable fixes (#13186, #13038).
Security and process isolation
Web pages run in sandboxed renderer processes, so a malicious page that takes over its renderer should be stuck there.
We kept fixing security issues from many sources, including ways around that sandbox. For example, a compromised renderer could ask the browser process to open any file on your computer. Now only a renderer showing local files can read them (#12582, #12590). Renderers could also fake a user click to open popups or read the clipboard. The browser process no longer trusts them on this (#12597).
We also split the browser into more processes, so a compromised one can reach less:
- Cross-site iframes get their own renderer by default (#12647), and so do cross-site popups (#12296).
- Each top-level site gets its own network process, and the HTTP cache and third-party cookies are kept separate per site (#13144, #12424).
- Each renderer has its own audio process (#12604) and image decoder (#12437).
Media and Windows
On Windows, video now plays and YouTube works (#12646, #13195). Hardware video decoding moved to its own process and now works on Linux through Vulkan (#12868). We also read MP4 files ourselves now instead of using FFmpeg, which fixes problems with seeking and buffering (#12641).
More C++ moved to Rust
LibJS’s runtime moved from C++ to Rust just before the JIT landed, so our JavaScript engine is now all Rust, apart from its flap interpreter and the garbage collector (#12492). The new Wasm engine is Rust as well. WebGL, 2D canvas, IndexedDB, Streams, and URL also moved over (#12699, #12935, #13287, #13083, #12998). We also deleted the C++ style computation, so style is now computed entirely in Rust (#12346).
Getting ready for alpha
Our first alpha is planned for later this year. This month we added:
-   Release builds:  macOS archives, Linux tarballs, .deb and .rpm packages, and Flatpak bundles (#13176, #13313, #13340).
- Crash reports: after a crash, you can review a report and choose to send it to us (#12298, #12342).
- A welcome page to pick your tab layout, search engine, and ad blocking (#12333).
- Reporting broken sites from inside the browser (#12880).
That’s it for October. Thanks for reading, and we’ll see you next month!

We rendered this page in Ladybird, using features that landed in October:
From the top left, that’s multi-column (#13026), display: grid-lanes for masonry (#13236), MathML (#13062, #13141), corner-shape (#12942), CSS Motion Path (#13027), much more of anchor positioning (#13021, #13079, #13166), and text-wrap: balance (#13461).
We also added:
-   CSS:  calc-size(), which lets heights animate to and from auto (#13006), plus vertical writing modes (#13103), zoom (#13237), the stretch sizing keyword (#13006), shape() and border-shape (#12942), field-sizing (#13050), view progress timelines and animation-range (#12943), and the start of SVG animation (#12823, #13498).
-   Web APIs and more:  the HTML Sanitizer API (#13185), Touch Events (#13249), Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (#12296), Paint Timing, Event Timing, Largest Contentful Paint (#13110), WebVTT cues (#12895), wide-gamut canvases (#13097), WebDriver BiDi (#13167), JavaScript’s using and await using (#13102), and many execCommand and contenteditable fixes (#13186, #13038).
Security and process isolation
Web pages run in sandboxed renderer processes, so a malicious page that takes over its renderer should be stuck there.
We kept fixing security issues from many sources, including ways around that sandbox. For example, a compromised renderer could ask the browser process to open any file on your computer. Now only a renderer showing local files can read them (#12582, #12590). Renderers could also fake a user click to open popups or read the clipboard. The browser process no longer trusts them on this (#12597).
We also split the browser into more processes, so a compromised one can reach less:
- Cross-site iframes get their own renderer by default (#12647), and so do cross-site popups (#12296).
- Each top-level site gets its own network process, and the HTTP cache and third-party cookies are kept separate per site (#13144, #12424).
- Each renderer has its own audio process (#12604) and image decoder (#12437).
Media and Windows
On Windows, video now plays and YouTube works (#12646, #13195). Hardware video decoding moved to its own process and now works on Linux through Vulkan (#12868). We also read MP4 files ourselves now instead of using FFmpeg, which fixes problems with seeking and buffering (#12641).
More C++ moved to Rust
LibJS’s runtime moved from C++ to Rust just before the JIT landed, so our JavaScript engine is now all Rust, apart from its flap interpreter and the garbage collector (#12492). The new Wasm engine is Rust as well. WebGL, 2D canvas, IndexedDB, Streams, and URL also moved over (#12699, #12935, #13287, #13083, #12998). We also deleted the C++ style computation, so style is now computed entirely in Rust (#12346).
Getting ready for alpha
Our first alpha is planned for later this year. This month we added:
-   Release builds:  macOS archives, Linux tarballs, .deb and .rpm packages, and Flatpak bundles (#13176, #13313, #13340).
- Crash reports: after a crash, you can review a report and choose to send it to us (#12298, #12342).
- A welcome page to pick your tab layout, search engine, and ad blocking (#12333).
- Reporting broken sites from inside the browser (#12880).
That’s it for October. Thanks for reading, and we’ll see you next month!

articles.title: God of War Laufey delayed until May
articles.body:
God of War Laufey’s release date is being delayed to May 20th, 2027, developer Santa Monica Studio announced today. It was set to launch on PlayStation 5 on February 16th.
God of War Laufey delayed until May
Santa Monica Studio’s next God of War game is now set for a May 20th release.
Here is Santa Monica Studio’s full message about the delay:
Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we’ve been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye’s journey through the Everywhen. We don’t take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans.
With this in mind, we’ve made the decision to delay God of War Laufey’s release to May 20th, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we’ll be back to share more updates soon!
Laufey stars Faye, the wife of usual God of War protagonist Kratos, and she is played again by Deborah Ann Woll. Based on a 23-minute gameplay reveal earlier this year, Laufey looks to play differently than the other recent God of War games, with more of a focus on acrobatic action.

articles.title: An end to buggy web apps
articles.body:
An end to buggy web apps
It is possible now to reliably and automatically detect and fix every bug which users are encountering on the web. This clearly hasn’t happened yet. Our mission at Replay is to bring it about.
A few ingredients are needed:
- A modern coding agent
- Observability to see every bug
- Observability to root cause each bug
- A harness wiring these together
The right observability is key to this process, as it is generally to the AI powered SDLC.
Agents need context to thrive, and observability is the context layer for agents to know how the app they are building actually behaves. When they don’t actually know what is going on, they start guessing, make mistakes, and things go downhill quickly. When they do know, they can confirm theories about the app’s behavior and stay on track.
Better observability drives better results.
Perfect Observability
Replay’s core technology is a time travel debugger for Chromium and Node.js. Forked versions of these runtimes capture non-deterministic inputs to the runtimes with low overhead, allowing the runtime to be replayed deterministically. Everything it did while recording can be recovered and unpacked into what is essentially a database, allowing agents to see every statement that was executed, the state at every point, every control and data dependency, and so on, with no loss of detail.
A time travel debugger provides perfect observability: every question about how the app behaved can be answered. With one in hand, agents never need to guess. They can figure out exactly what happened, work their way back to the actual root cause of a problem, and develop the right fix.
Replay QA
We launched Replay QA a few months ago as a drop in tool for finding and explaining every bug in an app, building on our debugger. QA explores and tests apps on its own or with guidance, and with new self healing capabilities can create recordings by reproducing user sessions from partial and redacted data. It processes the recordings it creates to spot a wide variety of bugs (from broken features to glitches, performance issues, security holes and so on) and for every bug identifies the root cause and supports its analysis with evidence drawn from the recording.
QA can also fix itself. Its entire backend is recorded, and when problems are detected (failures to spot a bug or root cause it accurately) those problems are debugged, fixed, and converted to a durable test case by a software factory.
As an experiment we ran QA on 40 apps that have won contests or otherwise been promoted by major app building tools (Lovable, Replit, Base44, Bolt.new, etc). We had Astra confirm and deduplicate findings and ended up with over 900 bugs, with the distribution below.
Example: dead button
For comparison we ran other QA tools on some of these apps. Below is a bug report from QA Wolf on one of the apps, CallVance. A download button doesn’t work. QA Wolf identifies and generates STR for the bug, but does not explain at all what is causing it.
An agent addressing this bug report has to read the code and guess what the root cause is. If it guesses wrong it will have to go through several repair cycles and might end up stuck and unable to fix the problem.
These problems are not specific to CallVance or QA Wolf. The products of app building tools are loaded with bugs, and QA’ing them without using a time travel debugger can only give limited information about the causes. Surface level observations from watching screen recordings or looking at network and console logs can sometimes suggest a cause, but can’t identify it definitively, and the agent is always left guessing.
Below is a report from Replay QA for the same dead button.
Replay QA identifies the exact problem: a missing onClick handler on the React component. QA identified the rendering function associated with the button, and produced evidence showing that function and the missing handler. An agent reviewing this report can cross check the root cause against the evidence, and fix the bug itself without guessing.
Example: layout shift
The technique above applies just as well to more complex bugs, including ones that are difficult to spot without recording based analysis. Below is a layout shift in the same CallVance app. While the app loads, a skeleton changes size and other controls on the page shift around on their own, impacting usability.
Below is the root cause from the report.
This report is more extensive and describes the root cause of the layout shift in reference to all the contributing factors, including the different React commits, the network requests made in between, and variable values in the component render functions. This detailed report provides an agent exactly what it needs to fix the layout shift properly.
What’s Next
Replay QA is generally available and free to try today. It’s easy to set up integrations including self healing user session analysis, github and agent connections, and scheduled runs to keep a close watch on your app according to your needs. We are continually improving QA and are working on incorporating backend recording generation and analysis more deeply for full stack time travel debugging.
QA is also available to use via API to generate recordings and analyze them for bugs. Contact us if you’re interested in integrating its capabilities directly into a product you’re building.

articles.title: Guerrilla Bike Lanes: San Francisco Makes Illicit Infrastructure Permanent
articles.body:
When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official.
The SFMTrA, a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:
- Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians.
- Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists.
- Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety.
Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones, which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.
“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement, “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.
Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.
City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.
In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).
Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress.

articles.title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
articles.body:
American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.
Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “compute campuses” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported.

articles.title: Mocktastic: A Meshtastic Node on Arduino
articles.body:
Mocktastic is a small, customizable Meshtastic-compatible LoRa client for ESP32 boards using ArduinoIDE environment. It is an educational and experimental implementation, not a fork of the official Meshtastic firmware. The project demonstrates how to build and decode Meshtastic packets in C++, and includes a working environmental-sensor example.
The firmware has two compile-time modes:
- DECODER provides an interactive serial shell for receiving, decoding, and sending text messages on configured Meshtastic channels and direct messages.
- SENSOR turns the board into a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor. It can
send measurements and respond to /dht messages on its configured private
channel.
The implementation targets the LilyGO T3 LoRa32 V1.6.1 (ESP32-PICO and SX1276) and is intended to be adapted to other compatible ESP32/LoRa hardware.
The project uses MBDTLS for the cryptographic part during the test phase and Nano-Protobuf as a lightweight protobuf encoder. The tests are written using Doctest’s lightweight C++ tests.
The repository root contains meshtastic_decoder/, which holds the firmware
and host-side tests:
I used Python’s unittest approach as a model for testing individual,
predictable units of logic. The project keeps protocol and utility logic
separate from hardware effects so it can be exercised on a development
machine. The tests themselves are written with the lightweight doctest
framework and compile with bundled
test dependencies.
From meshtastic_decoder, run:
cd meshtastic_decoder
make test
The Makefile builds and runs the tests as one step. Tests cover the
platform-independent functions, cryptography, Meshtastic packet handling, and
shell parsing; changes to radio or sensor behavior should also be checked on
the target hardware. To build the API documentation, install Doxygen and
Graphviz, then run make doxygen from meshtastic_decoder/; the generated
documentation is written to meshtastic_decoder/docs/html/.
You need an ESP32 board and a Semtech SX1276-family LoRa radio. The SENSOR variant also requires a DHT22. The tested board is the LilyGO T3 LoRa32 V1.6.1, which integrates the ESP32 and LoRa radio.
Install Arduino IDE, download or clone this repository, and open
meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino. Install these libraries through
the Arduino Library Manager:
- LoRa by Sandeep Mistry
- Adafruit Unified Sensor
- DHT sensor library by Adafruit
open build_opt.h and put your hard-coded filepath. It should result like this: "Hard/coded/path/…/Mocktastic/meshtastic_decoder/nanopb_meshtastic/src"
=== LoRa pins
Check your board’s specifications to identify the corresponding pins. The following mapping is for the LilyGO T3 V1.6.1:
Enter the pins for your board in the LoRa pin definitions in
meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino:
#define LORA_SCK   5
#define LORA_MISO  19
#define LORA_MOSI  27
#define LORA_SS    18
#define LORA_RST   23
#define LORA_DIO0  26
Use the following table as a reference for Meshtastic radio presets. Confirm that your selected preset and frequency are supported in your region.
The sketch’s default is EU Medium Fast, configured as follows:
LoRa.begin(869525024);
LoRa.setSpreadingFactor(9);
LoRa.setSignalBandwidth(250E3);
LoRa.setCodingRate4(5);
LoRa.setSyncWord(0x2B);
LoRa.setPreambleLength(16);
LoRa.enableCrc();
Always verify local radio regulations before transmitting. In the Meshtastic documentation’s Overview page, use Radio Settings and its Frequency Slot Calculator to select a channel and slot and determine the corresponding frequency. Use that frequency in the sketch and make sure it matches the other nodes.
Before compiling, configure PublicChannel, PrivateChannel, Admn, and
Device in meshtastic_decoder/keys.h:
- For PublicChannel, enter the name and key of the public channel used at the
selected frequency. The channel name corresponds to the radio preset (for
example, MediumFast).
- For PrivateChannel, enter the name and key of the private channel used for
messages.
- For Admn, enter the name or node ID and public key of the main node from
which you will read messages. Do not put a private key in this entry.
- For Device, enter this node’s name, public key, and private key.
Read the channel configuration and node details using the Meshtastic software
connected to the relevant node. The Channel structure contains name and
key; Friend contains name and publicKey; and User contains name,
publicKey, and privateKey, in that order. Keys must be hexadecimal strings.
Meshtastic may provide them in Base64; convert them to hexadecimal with
b64StrToHexStr() before adding them to the configuration.
Use your own credentials and keep private keys and channel keys secret. Do not publish them in a public repository.
The sketch selects its mode at compile time. Near the top of
meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino, keep DECODER defined for the
serial shell, or replace it with SENSOR for the DHT22 sensor variant:
#define DECODER
For the sensor build, replace that line with:
#define SENSOR
Build and upload the sketch with Arduino IDE for your selected ESP32 board.
The DECODER variant is operated over the serial connection. Open the serial monitor at 115200 baud. Its commands are:
For example, send /pub 42 is the answer to write on the public channel.
To send hello, world! on the private channel, use
/cantine hello, world!.
To enable direct messages with Admn, first send /send_key. This sends this
node’s public key so that the official Meshtastic node can establish a private
conversation. Then send a direct message with /admn hello, world!.
The SENSOR variant has no interactive shell. It can only be controlled by
sending a Meshtastic message on the private channel configured in keys.h.
Send /dht on that channel to make the sensor measure temperature and
humidity; it sends the result back as a text message on the same channel.
Connect the DHT22 data pin to GPIO 21. A battery is also required for standalone operation.
Keep protocol and parsing logic separate from hardware effects where possible.
The portable logic is exercised by host-side tests, while the .ino sketch
handles radio, serial, GPIO, and sensor interactions.
For a new shell command, follow the existing pattern in
meshtastic_decoder/lora_shell.h and meshtastic_decoder/lora_shell.cpp: add
the command to the parser and command enum, then handle it in the dispatcher
in meshtastic_decoder/meshtastic_decoder.ino. For higher-level packet
operations, start with the functions in lora_shell and the interfaces in
meshtastic.h; use functions.h for lower-level helpers.
Run make test from meshtastic_decoder/ after changing platform-independent
logic. Hardware behavior still needs to be verified on the target board and
against compatible Meshtastic nodes.
This code is a learning and prototyping project. It has limited field testing, does not provide the reliability or power efficiency of the official Meshtastic firmware, and is not recommended for safety-critical or production use. Its SENSOR battery life, channel handling, and regional radio configuration may need further work for a particular application.

articles.title: The Internals of PostgreSQL
articles.body:
After a temporary stay in Japan to focus on my health and personal responsibilities, I am fully recovered, ready, and excited to work abroad again.
I am highly interested in returning to Europe, as well as opportunities in the Southern Hemisphere and Southeast Asia.
Looking for:
- Challenging tasks in PostgreSQL.
- Roles offering international visa sponsorship OR Remote work that supports a digital nomad lifestyle.
If your team is hiring, let’s connect! Please feel free to reach out via e-Mail(hironobu @ interdb.jp or interdb.mx @ gmail.com) or DM.
What’s New
- 26 Sep 2026: 11th Anniversary! This content was launched on 26 September 2015.
- 28 Jun 2026: Section 8.5, “Asynchronous I/O in PostgreSQL” Published.
- 1 May 2026: Chapter 12, “Logical Replication” (Beta Version) Published.
- 14 Dec 2024: Added Conflicts in Section 11.2.4.
The Internals of PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world.
It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult.
The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL.
This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier.
Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019.
This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015.
- Chapter 1. Database Cluster, Databases and Tables
- Chapter 2. Process and Memory Architecture
- Chapter 3. Query Processing
- Chapter 4. Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW)
- Chapter 5. Concurrency Control
- Chapter 6. VACUUM Processing
- Chapter 7. Heap Only Tuple (HOT) and Index-Only Scans
- Chapter 8. Buffer Manager
- Chapter 9. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
- Chapter 10. Online Backup and Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)
- Chapter 11. Streaming Replication
- Chapter 12. Logical Replication (Beta Version)
Author
Hironobu SUZUKI
I am a software programmer/engineer, the author of:
I graduated from graduate school in information engineering (M.S. in Information Engineering), have worked for several companies as a software developer and technical manager/director. I published seven books in the fields of database and system integration (4 PostgreSQL books and 3 MySQL books). In June 2019, the Chinese book of this documentation was published.
As a director of the Japan PostgreSQL Users Group (2010-2016), I organized the largest (non-commercial) technical seminar/lecture on PostgreSQL in Japan for more than six years, and also served as the program committee chair of the Japan PostgreSQL Conference in 2013 and as a member in 2008 and 2009.
In June 2022, my interview article was published in “PostgreSQL person of the week”.
Cuando era joven, vivió en Sudamérica por unos años. Recientemente, a veces vuelve a allí.
I am seeking a remote position focused on the application of ML and AI technologies to DBMS. For personal reasons, I will be living in Japan for several years.
Contact
Please read the following FAQ before sending messages.
After reading, send a message to my twitter in public.
If you use email, please provide at least two SNS addresses (e.g. LinkedIn, Twitter) for verification purposes. Due to the XZ backdoor incident, I no longer accept contact from anonymous individuals.
Copyright

For any inquiries regarding the use of this documentation or any of its figures, please contact me.
Exception Educational institutions can use this documentation freely.
